practice_questions.text: A student tests the melting point of a white powder. The powder starts to melt at 48°C and is fully melted by 57°C. The accepted melting point of the pure compound is 52°C. What can the student conclude about the purity of the powder?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the powder is impure/a mixture (1), because a pure substance would melt at a single fixed temperature, but this sample melts over a range (1). Secure: states impure with reference to melting range. Developing: states impure but explanation is weak. Emerging: no link between evidence and conclusion.

practice_questions.text: A student runs paper chromatography on a food dye sample. The solvent front travels 9.0 cm. Spot A travels 6.3 cm. Calculate the Rf value of spot A and identify whether spot A could be the same substance as a reference compound with Rf = 0.70.
practice_questions.marks: Rf = 6.3 ÷ 9.0 = 0.70 (1 mark for correct calculation); yes, spot A could be the same substance as the reference compound because their Rf values are equal (1 mark). Mastering: correct calculation and reasoned comparison. Secure: correct answer. Developing: correct formula used but arithmetic error. Emerging: formula not recalled.

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper chromatography could be used to determine whether a sample of green food colouring contains more than one dye. Include the key steps and how you would interpret the result.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: spot sample on pencil baseline on chromatography paper; place in solvent below the baseline; allow solvent to rise (1); remove and mark solvent front with pencil; calculate Rf values (1); if multiple spots appear at different heights, the colouring contains more than one dye; a pure dye would give a single spot (1). Secure: three steps described. Developing: two steps with partial interpretation. Emerging: one step.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fractional distillation rather than simple distillation is used to separate the components of crude oil.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: crude oil contains many components with similar boiling points (1); simple distillation cannot separate liquids with close boiling points as they evaporate at similar temperatures (1); the fractionating column allows repeated condensation and evaporation, progressively separating liquids by boiling point into fractions (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: mentions different boiling points without explaining how separation works.

practice_questions.text: Background question — mass spectrometry is not named in the specification for this course. A crime scene analyst uses mass spectrometry to identify an unknown white powder. Explain how mass spectrometry works and why it is preferred over a melting point test in this context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: mass spectrometry ionises molecules and measures mass-to-charge ratios of fragments (1); the molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass (1); mass spectrometry can identify substances from very small samples with high sensitivity (1); a melting point test only works if you know what you expect and have enough material to observe a clear melting range (1); in forensic work where the identity is unknown, mass spectrometry identifies without prior knowledge and can detect trace amounts (1). Secure: 3–4 points. Developing: 2 points. Emerging: 1 point.

practice_questions.text: Outline a method to obtain pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from a mixture of copper sulfate dissolved in water.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: heat the copper sulfate solution to evaporate most of the water (1); remove from heat and leave to cool slowly — crystals form as solubility decreases (1); filter the crystals to separate them from the remaining solution (residue on filter paper, filtrate discarded) (1); dry the crystals gently, e.g. by leaving on filter paper in a warm place or a low oven (1). Secure: all four steps. Developing: three steps. Emerging: one or two steps.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of pathogen that causes each of the following diseases: (a) influenza  (b) malaria  (c) athlete's foot  (d) tobacco mosaic virus in plants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: all four correct — (a) virus, (b) protist, (c) fungus, (d) virus. Two marks for four correct. Secure: three correct. Developing: two correct. Emerging: one correct.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the malaria parasite is transmitted from one human host to another.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the malaria parasite (Plasmodium, a protist) is carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes; the mosquito bites an infected person and takes up the parasite; the mosquito later bites another person, transferring the parasite into their bloodstream; the parasite infects red blood cells. Secure: mosquito as vector identified; transmission mechanism described; one step vague. Developing: states mosquito bites transmit malaria without identifying the parasite type or process. Emerging: vague reference to insects spreading disease.

practice_questions.text: Explain why viruses are more difficult to treat than bacterial infections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: viruses reproduce inside host cells using the cell's own machinery; antibiotics target structures specific to bacteria (e.g. cell wall) but cannot kill viruses without damaging host cells; antiviral drugs exist but are harder to design because of this; the body's immune system must largely fight off viral infections. Secure: states viruses are inside cells and antibiotics don't work on viruses; mechanism of why partially explained. Developing: states antibiotics don't work on viruses but does not explain why. Emerging: states viruses are hard to treat without scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe three non-specific defences that protect the human body against pathogens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any three from — skin (impermeable physical barrier); mucus and cilia in airways (traps and sweeps pathogens away from lungs); stomach acid (low pH kills ingested pathogens); tears/saliva lysozyme (enzyme breaks down bacterial cell walls); gut bacteria (compete with pathogens). Each defence described with its mechanism. Three defences with mechanisms = four marks. Secure: three defences named but one or two mechanisms missing. Developing: two defences with mechanisms. Emerging: one or two defences named without mechanisms.

practice_questions.text: A plant disease is spreading rapidly through a local woodland, causing trees to show leaf discolouration and reduced growth. A scientist suspects a fungal pathogen. Describe how the scientist could identify whether the pathogen is fungal, and explain one method to prevent further spread.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes taking a sample from an infected plant; culturing on agar; microscopy to identify fungal structures (hyphae, spores); or DNA analysis to confirm identity; notes that correct identification is essential before choosing a control strategy; prevention method: removing and destroying infected trees, preventing movement of infected material, chemical fungicide treatment, or biological control — with mechanism explained and reliability considered. Secure: identification method described adequately; prevention method with partial reasoning. Developing: mentions culture or microscopy but method is vague; prevention stated without explanation. Emerging: general reference to 'testing' without scientific method.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a communicable and a non-communicable disease, with one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: communicable = caused by a pathogen, can spread between organisms (e.g. influenza/Salmonella/HIV); non-communicable = not caused by an infection, cannot be passed on (e.g. type 2 diabetes/cancer/cardiovascular disease). Both defined with examples. Secure: both types defined correctly; one example missing. Developing: one type defined correctly. Emerging: vague distinction without reference to pathogens or examples.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the relative formula mass (M<sub>r</sub>) of sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. (A<sub>r</sub>: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16.)
practice_questions.marks: Award: M<sub>r</sub> = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 98. Accept correct calculation only.

practice_questions.text: How many moles are present in 8 g of magnesium? (A<sub>r</sub> of Mg = 24.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: moles equation stated and correct answer 0.33 mol (or 1/3 mol) with unit.
Secure: correct method, minor rounding error accepted.
Developing: equation recalled but numerical error.
Emerging: equation not recalled.

practice_questions.text: A sample contains 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 100). Calculate the mass of the sample and explain what is meant by one mole.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g (1), one mole defined as 6.0 × 10²³ particles (1), links mole to mass using M<sub>r</sub> (1).
Secure: correct mass, definition incomplete.
Developing: mass correct but mole not defined.
Emerging: partial attempt at calculation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the percentage by mass of nitrogen in two fertilisers: ammonium nitrate (NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 80) and urea (CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 60). Which contains a higher percentage of nitrogen? (A<sub>r</sub>: N = 14.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> has 2 N atoms: percentage = (2 × 14 ÷ 80) × 100 = 35% (1); urea has 2 N atoms: percentage = (2 × 14 ÷ 60) × 100 = 46.7% (1); correct comparison that urea has higher nitrogen content (1); correct method shown for both (1).
Secure: both percentages correct, comparison stated.
Developing: one correct percentage, method shown.
Emerging: percentage equation stated but not applied correctly.

practice_questions.text: When 2.4 g of magnesium ribbon is burned in air, 4.0 g of magnesium oxide is formed. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted. Explain whether mass has been conserved in this reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass of oxygen = 4.0 − 2.4 = 1.6 g (1), mass is conserved because no atoms are created or destroyed (1), the extra mass came from oxygen in the air combining with magnesium (1).
Secure: correct mass of oxygen, partial explanation.
Developing: mass calculated but explanation incomplete.
Emerging: calculation only or explanation only.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the reaction of calcium carbonate with acid. The student measures the mass of the flask and contents at the start and end and finds the total mass has decreased. Using your knowledge of chemical reactions and conservation of mass, explain this observation and suggest how the experiment could be modified to demonstrate that mass is actually conserved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass conservation stated as a principle (1), identifies CO<sub>2</sub> gas escaping as the cause of apparent mass decrease (2), modification suggested e.g. collecting gas or using a sealed system (1), clear explanation that if gas is captured the total mass would be unchanged (2).
Secure: principle stated, gas escape identified, modification present but not fully justified.
Developing: gas escape mentioned, limited explanation.
Emerging: identifies a mass change without scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the 'plum pudding' model of the atom?
A) A tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons in fixed energy levels
B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it
C) A solid, indivisible sphere with no internal structure
D) A nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons orbiting freely
practice_questions.marks: B) A positively charged sphere with electrons embedded throughout it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the experiment that provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom, and who carried it out.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Geiger–Marsden (gold foil / alpha scattering) experiment (1) carried out by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford's direction / by Rutherford (1).
Secure: Names gold foil experiment and Rutherford.
Developing: Names either the experiment or the scientist.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened in the gold foil experiment and explain what this showed about the structure of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Most alpha particles passed straight through (1) showing the atom is mostly empty space; a small number were deflected at large angles (1) showing there is a concentrated positive charge at the centre; this tiny, dense centre is the nucleus (1).
Secure: Two observations with correct interpretation.
Developing: States particles passed through or were deflected but does not fully interpret.
Emerging: Vague description of the experiment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of the atomic model from Dalton to Bohr is an example of how scientific knowledge develops over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Each model was accepted as the best explanation of available evidence at the time (1); Dalton's solid sphere was replaced when Thomson discovered electrons (1); Thomson's plum pudding was replaced when Rutherford's alpha scattering results could not be explained by a diffuse positive charge (1); Bohr modified Rutherford's model when it could not explain why electrons didn't lose energy and spiral inward (1); models are revised only when new evidence forces revision — they are not discarded arbitrarily (1).
Secure: Four points with clear sense of evidence driving change.
Developing: Two to three changes described with partial explanation.
Emerging: Names scientists without explaining the process.

practice_questions.text: Compare the Rutherford nuclear model and the Bohr model of the atom. What problem did Bohr's model solve that Rutherford's could not?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both models have electrons orbiting a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (1); Rutherford's model does not specify where electrons can orbit (1); Bohr proposed electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) and do not emit energy within a level (1); this solved the problem of why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus under classical physics (1).
Secure: Three points with correct comparison.
Developing: Describes one model adequately.
Emerging: Names both models without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain how James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron in 1932 completed the nuclear model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Before 1932, the nucleus was thought to contain only protons (1); the mass of most atoms was greater than could be explained by protons alone (1); Chadwick discovered a neutral particle (the neutron) with a mass similar to a proton, which accounted for the extra mass and completed the picture of the nucleus containing both protons and neutrons (1).
Secure: Problem and solution both addressed.
Developing: States neutron was discovered and adds to nucleus but does not explain the mass problem.
Emerging: Names neutron without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: State what magnification means.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The number of times larger the image appears compared with the actual object / the ratio of image size to actual size.
Secure: Image is larger than real object by a set amount.
Developing: Something about the image being bigger.
Emerging: Vague or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: A plant cell is drawn in a biology textbook. The drawn width of the cell is 36 mm and the actual width of the cell is 0.09 mm. Calculate the magnification used. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 36 ÷ 0.09 = ×400. (Both marks: correct formula applied + correct answer.)
Secure: Correct formula and method but minor arithmetic error; or correct answer with insufficient working shown.
Developing: Formula recalled but values substituted incorrectly.
Emerging: Attempt at calculation but no correct formula shown.

practice_questions.text: An electron microscope image shows a mitochondrion with a drawn length of 60 mm. The magnification is ×12,000. Calculate the actual length of the mitochondrion in micrometres (µm). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 60 ÷ 12,000 = 0.005 mm; convert: 0.005 mm × 1,000 = 5 µm. (All three marks: rearrangement [1], calculation in mm [1], correct conversion to µm [1].)
Secure: Correct rearrangement and calculation but conversion step missing or minor error.
Developing: Rearrangement attempted but magnification used as multiplier rather than divisor.
Emerging: Some values substituted but no clear method.

practice_questions.text: Convert the following measurements: (a) 0.25 mm into µm; (b) 8,500 nm into µm; (c) 2 µm into nm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) 250 µm; (b) 8.5 µm; (c) 2,000 nm. (One mark per correct answer.)
Secure: Two out of three correct.
Developing: One correct conversion; others show confusion between × and ÷ steps.
Emerging: Attempts made but all conversions incorrect.

practice_questions.text: A student uses a light microscope and then an electron microscope to study a cell. Suggest two advantages of using an electron microscope rather than a light microscope when studying organelles such as mitochondria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two advantages, each with explanation: (1) Higher magnification — electron microscopes can magnify far more than light microscopes, so organelles appear larger and more detail is visible. (2) Greater resolution — electron microscopes can distinguish between structures that are very close together, whereas light microscopes cannot; this means individual features of organelles (e.g. cristae of mitochondria) can be seen. [2 marks per advantage: 1 for the advantage, 1 for the explanation.]
Secure: Two advantages stated with partial explanation.
Developing: One advantage with explanation, or two advantages without explanation.
Emerging: One advantage stated without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A scientist claims that the development of the electron microscope was essential for improving our understanding of sub-cellular structures. Evaluate this claim, referring to the limitations of light microscopes and the types of evidence that electron microscopy provided.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates both sides clearly. Arguments for: electron microscopes provide magnification up to ×1,000,000 (vs ~×1,500 for light), enabling detailed images of organelles; resolution is high enough to show internal structure of mitochondria (cristae) and chloroplasts (grana); this led to understanding of how structure relates to function; light microscopes cannot resolve structures closer than about 200 nm, so organelles below this size are invisible. Balancing point: light microscopes allow study of living cells; electron microscopes require dead, stained specimens. Conclusion: the claim is well-supported — electron microscopy genuinely transformed understanding that was impossible before its development. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Both types of microscope discussed with relevant points; some attempt at evaluative conclusion.
Developing: Descriptive comparison with limited evaluation.
Emerging: One or two relevant points about microscopes with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Give one example of a Newton's third law force pair.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size, opposite in direction and the same type / act on different objects.
1 mark: a valid example, e.g. a book pushes down on a table (contact force); the table pushes up on the book with an equal contact force — accept any correct pair identifying the two objects and directions.

practice_questions.text: A cyclist of mass 70 kg, including the bicycle, experiences a driving force of 280 N from pedalling and a resistive force of 80 N from air resistance. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Resultant force = 280 − 80 = 200 N [1 mark for correct resultant]
\(a = F/m = 200/70 = 2.86\) m/s\(^2\) (accept 2.9 m/s\(^2\)) [1 mark for correct answer with unit].

Common error: using 280 N rather than the resultant force.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between mass and weight, using an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states mass is measured in kg and weight in N.
Secure: mass is the amount of matter in an object; it does not change with location, measured in kg. Weight is the gravitational force on an object; it depends on the gravitational field strength at that location, measured in N.
Mastering: as Secure, plus gives a numerical example (e.g. a 50 kg student weighs 500 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) but only 80 N on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg); their mass remains 50 kg).

[1 mark: mass = amount of matter, kg, does not change; 1 mark: weight = gravitational force, N, depends on location; 1 mark: valid numerical example]

practice_questions.text: Draw a labelled free body diagram for a skydiver falling at terminal velocity. Use your diagram to explain why the skydiver is not accelerating.
practice_questions.marks:
Diagram [2 marks]: two arrows from the skydiver — weight downward, labelled W (or weight, or mg); drag/air resistance upward, labelled F_drag (or air resistance); both arrows equal in length.

Explanation [2 marks]: the resultant force is zero because weight equals air resistance; by Newton's first law / Newton's second law with F = 0, acceleration = 0, so the skydiver falls at constant (terminal) velocity.

Emerging: draws arrows but does not label or explain.
Mastering: links explicitly to F = ma with F_resultant = 0 → a = 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Newton's discovery of the universal nature of gravity — that the same force causes objects to fall on Earth and keeps the Moon in orbit — is considered an important example of creative thinking in science.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states Newton connected Earth's gravity to the Moon's orbit.
Secure: before Newton, these were considered unrelated phenomena; Newton's insight (IaS3) was to propose that the same mathematical law — gravity decreasing with distance squared — could explain both falling apples and planetary orbits; this required imagination beyond what the observations alone suggested.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that good scientific ideas go beyond the data and make testable predictions; Newton's law correctly predicted the orbits of other planets and eventually led to the discovery of Neptune through orbital anomalies — demonstrating how a creative model can generate new science.

[1 mark: identifies what Newton connected; 1 mark: explains why it required imagination/creativity; 1 mark: notes the law makes testable predictions; 1 mark: gives a specific consequence (e.g. planetary orbit prediction); 1 mark: links to how models in science develop with evidence (IaS3)]

practice_questions.text:
A crate of mass 120 kg is pushed along a flat surface by a force of 360 N. It moves at constant velocity.
(a) What is the resultant force on the crate?
(b) Calculate the friction force acting on the crate.
(c) If the pushing force increases to 480 N while friction stays the same, calculate the new acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Zero [1 mark] — constant velocity means no acceleration, so resultant force = 0 (Newton's first law).

(b) If resultant = 0, friction = driving force = 360 N [1 mark].

(c) Resultant = 480 − 360 = 120 N [1 mark]
\(a = F/m = 120/120 = 1\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for correct unit].

Emergng: correctly answers (a) only.
Secure: correctly answers all three with working shown.
Mastering: explicitly justifies (a) with Newton's first law and links friction = 360 N to equilibrium argument. [1 mark for clear logical justification in (a)/(b)]

practice_questions.text: A 1500 W hair dryer is used for 4 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred by the hair dryer. Give your answer in joules.
practice_questions.marks: Convert time: 4 minutes = 240 s [1]. \(E = P \times t = 1500 \times 240 = 360\,000\) J (360 kJ) [1].

practice_questions.text: An electric motor receives 800 J of electrical energy and transfers 600 J as useful kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency of the motor and state what happens to the remaining energy.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 600 ÷ 800 = 0.75 (75%) [1+1 for correct substitution and answer]. The remaining 200 J (25%) is dissipated [1] as thermal energy to the surroundings [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable energy source. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Renewable: can be replenished within a human timescale / will not run out [1]; example such as wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal or biofuel [1]. Non-renewable: cannot be replenished within a human timescale [1]; example such as coal, oil, gas or nuclear fuel [1]. (Any two marks from four bullet points.)

practice_questions.text: Compare the environmental impacts of generating electricity using fossil fuels and using wind turbines.
practice_questions.marks: Fossil fuels: release carbon dioxide when burned [1]; this contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming [1]. Wind turbines: produce no carbon dioxide during generation [1]; but visual impact on landscape, potential noise, and effects on local wildlife are concerns [1]. (Accept other valid environmental comparisons.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity from power stations is transmitted at high voltage through the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks: Transmitting at high voltage reduces the current needed to transfer the same power [1]. Lower current means less energy is dissipated as thermal energy in the cables (energy losses are lower) [1]. This makes transmission more efficient over long distances [1].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of nuclear power as an energy source for generating electricity. Consider both the advantages and the disadvantages in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that nuclear power is a non-renewable but low-CO2 source; explains that it provides reliable, on-demand generation unlike intermittent renewables; discusses the risks including radioactive waste (long-lived, difficult to dispose of) and potential for serious accidents; considers economic factors (high construction cost, long build time); weighs advantages against disadvantages and reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Gives at least two clear advantages and two disadvantages with brief explanation; attempts a conclusion.
Developing: Lists some advantages and disadvantages without clearly weighing them.
Emerging: Makes one or two simple points without evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals can be extracted from its ore by reduction with carbon?
A) Potassium
B) Sodium
C) Aluminium
D) Copper
practice_questions.marks: D) Copper [1 mark] — copper is below carbon in the reactivity series.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'displacement reaction' and give one example using named metals.
practice_questions.marks: A reaction where a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound [1]; e.g. zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper (or other valid example with correct reactivity direction) [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how iron is extracted from iron ore in a blast furnace. Include the names of the raw materials added and the process by which iron is produced.
practice_questions.marks: Iron ore (haematite/Fe₂O₃), coke (carbon) and limestone are added [1]; hot air is blasted in and carbon burns to form carbon monoxide [1]; carbon (or carbon monoxide) reduces iron oxide to molten iron, which is tapped from the bottom of the furnace [1].

practice_questions.text: A mining company wants to recover copper from a large area of land where the ore concentration is too low for conventional mining. Explain how phytomining could be used to extract the copper, including what happens to the copper after the plants are harvested.
practice_questions.marks: Hyperaccumulator plants are grown on the low-grade ore / soil [1]; the plants absorb copper ions through their roots and accumulate them in leaves/stems [1]; the plants are harvested and burned / incinerated [1]; copper compounds are concentrated in the ash and processed to obtain the metal [1].

practice_questions.text: A student compares extracting copper by smelting (heating ore with carbon) with bioleaching. Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of bioleaching from both an economic and an environmental perspective.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: Environmental advantages of bioleaching — avoids SO₂ air pollution from smelting [1]; can use low-grade ore that would otherwise be uneconomical [1]; Environmental disadvantages — produces acidic leachate that can pollute water sources [1]; requires management to prevent contamination [1]; Economic: lower energy costs and avoids expensive smelting equipment [1]; however, process is slow and requires bacterial maintenance [1]. Secure: four points with some weighing of evidence. Developing: two relevant points without comparative evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the reactivity series, why magnesium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution but copper does not displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution. Include the ionic equation for the displacement reaction between magnesium and copper sulfate.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: magnesium is higher in the reactivity series than copper [1]; more reactive metals displace less reactive metals from their compounds [1]; copper cannot displace magnesium because copper is less reactive [1]; ionic equation: Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu [1]; Mg is oxidised (loses electrons) and Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains electrons) [1]. Secure: first four points. Developing: states Mg more reactive and writes word equation only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the main gas in Earth's early atmosphere?
A) Oxygen
B) Nitrogen
C) Carbon dioxide
D) Argon
practice_questions.marks: C) Carbon dioxide [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'volcanic outgassing'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that volcanic outgassing is the release of gases from magma/volcanoes (1) and gives examples of gases released such as carbon dioxide, water vapour or nitrogen (1).
Secure: Names volcanic release of gases but gives only one example.
Developing: Vague reference to volcanoes releasing something.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process by which oxygen levels in the atmosphere increased over geological time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that early photosynthetic organisms (e.g. algae/cyanobacteria) (1) used carbon dioxide and released oxygen as a byproduct (1) and that this process occurred over billions of years, gradually building up oxygen (1).
Secure: Identifies photosynthesis and oxygen release with some sense of timescale.
Developing: Mentions photosynthesis but explanation incomplete.
Emerging: Simple mention of organisms or oxygen with no mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (i) CO₂ dissolved in the oceans (1) and was then locked into carbonate rocks or shells of marine organisms (1). (ii) Photosynthesis by early organisms used CO₂ (1) and produced oxygen instead (1).
Secure: Both processes named with partial development.
Developing: One process described adequately.
Emerging: Vague reference to CO₂ decreasing.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'Scientists have directly measured the composition of Earth's early atmosphere.' Evaluate this claim and explain how scientists actually obtain evidence about the early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly challenges the claim — the early atmosphere cannot be directly observed (1). Names at least two indirect evidence sources, e.g. ancient rock chemistry (1), composition of present-day volcanic gases (1), comparison with Mars/Venus atmospheres (1). Explains why multiple independent lines of evidence are needed to build confidence in a model (1).
Secure: Challenges claim and names two evidence types.
Developing: Challenges claim and gives one evidence type.
Emerging: Vague challenge with no supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Background question — the ozone layer is not named in the specification for this course. Explain why the formation of the ozone layer was significant for the development of life on Earth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that rising oxygen levels allowed ozone (⁠⁠O₃) to form from O₂ in the upper atmosphere (1); ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun (1); without the ozone layer, UV radiation would damage DNA and prevent complex life from surviving on land (1); the ozone layer therefore allowed organisms to move from ocean environments onto land (1); this opened new ecological niches and enabled the evolution of far greater biodiversity (1); links back to the fundamental role of photosynthesis in producing the oxygen that made the ozone layer possible (1).
Secure: Four of the above points with logical connections.
Developing: Two to three points, some logical flow.
Emerging: One point, limited development.

practice_questions.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: all travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; all are transverse waves; all transfer energy; all can travel through a vacuum (do not need a medium) — 1 mark each. Mastering: two distinct properties correctly stated. Secure: two properties. Developing: one correct property. Emerging: vague or incorrect statement.

practice_questions.text: A patient needs a chest X-ray. Explain one benefit and one risk of using X-rays for this medical purpose, and describe how the risk is managed using the ALARA principle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefit — X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense structures, enabling diagnosis of fractures, infections, or tumours (2); risk — X-rays are ionising radiation that can damage DNA and potentially cause cancer (2); ALARA — the dose is kept to the minimum needed for a clear image; staff use lead shielding and limit frequency of exposure; benefit of diagnosis outweighs small risk of a single X-ray (2). Secure: 4–5 marks. Developing: 2–3 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves, referring to ionisation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gamma rays have a much higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) than radio waves (1); higher frequency means more energy per wave — enough to remove electrons from atoms (ionise them) (1); ionisation can damage DNA in cells, potentially causing mutations or cancer; radio waves do not have enough energy to ionise and are considered non-ionising (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how ultraviolet radiation is both useful and potentially harmful. Refer to scientific evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: UV is useful — it causes fluorescence used in security marking and detecting forged banknotes; used in fluorescent lamps; triggers vitamin D production in skin (1+1); UV is harmful — overexposure causes sunburn; repeated overexposure damages DNA in skin cells, increasing risk of skin cancer (1); the evidence linking UV exposure to increased skin cancer rates is well-established from epidemiological studies (1); this illustrates that the same property (energy sufficient to excite electrons) underlies both uses and risks (1). Secure: 3–4 marks. Developing: 2 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties and uses of X-rays and infrared radiation. Include wavelength, frequency, and one use of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: X-rays have shorter wavelength and higher frequency than infrared (1); X-rays are ionising — used in medical imaging to show bones (1); infrared has longer wavelength and lower frequency; it is non-ionising (1); infrared is used in remote controls, thermal imaging, or optical fibre communication (1). Secure: all four points. Developing: three points. Emerging: two points.

practice_questions.text: Describe an investigation a student could carry out to compare the rate of infrared emission from surfaces with different colours and textures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: use a Leslie cube (or beakers with differently coloured surfaces: matt black, shiny silver) filled with hot water (1); place an infrared detector at a fixed, equal distance from each surface (1); record the infrared reading for each surface under identical conditions (same water temperature, same distance) (1); compare results — matt black surface should emit most infrared (1). Secure: all four stages. Developing: three stages. Emerging: two stages.

practice_questions.text: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is travelling at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Describe what happens to the stores of energy when a ball is thrown vertically upwards and then falls back to its starting height. Ignore air resistance.
practice_questions.marks: As the ball rises, kinetic energy decreases and gravitational potential energy increases by the same amount [1 mark]. As it falls, GPE converts back to KE; at the starting height the KE equals the original value [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that KE converts to GPE (or vice versa) but does not address both directions or conservation.

practice_questions.text: A crane lifts a 200 kg steel beam vertically by 15 m in 30 seconds. Calculate the power output of the crane's motor. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Attempts GPE or power calculation but makes an error in one step.

practice_questions.text: A car of mass 1,200 kg accelerates from rest to a speed of 20 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy gained. Then suggest why the engine must supply more energy than this value during the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks: E_k = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 0.5 × 1200 × 400 = 240,000 J [2 marks]. The engine must supply more energy because some energy is transferred to the surroundings by friction (between tyres and road and within engine parts) and by air resistance, so not all the engine's energy output becomes useful kinetic energy [1 mark — any suitable reason]. Dissipated energy ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct KE and identifies one energy loss mechanism.
Developing: Correct KE but does not explain energy loss, or vice versa.

practice_questions.text: A rollercoaster car of mass 800 kg is at the top of a drop at a height of 45 m above the ground. It starts from rest. Calculate the speed of the car at the bottom of the drop, assuming no energy is lost to friction or air resistance. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks: GPE at top = mgh = 800 × 10 × 45 = 360,000 J [1 mark]. This all converts to KE at the bottom: ½mv² = 360,000, so v² = (2 × 360,000) ÷ 800 = 900 [1 mark]; v = √900 = 30 m/s [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Calculates GPE correctly but cannot rearrange KE equation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'a heavier car is always more dangerous in a collision than a lighter car at the same speed.' Use physics to support and challenge this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates or compares KE using E_k = ½mv² for both cases; notes that at the same speed a heavier car has greater KE so more energy must be dissipated in a collision (supports the claim). Challenges by noting that speed is squared — a lighter car at twice the speed has four times the KE of the heavier car at the original speed, so speed is actually more significant than mass. Reaches a justified conclusion: the statement is partially true but speed is the dominant factor because of the v² relationship.
Secure: Correctly identifies KE depends on both mass and speed; compares the effect qualitatively; some reference to the equation.
Developing: Identifies that both mass and speed affect KE but does not use the equation to evaluate relative importance.
Emerging: States that heavier objects are more dangerous with no reference to KE equation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes aerobic respiration?
A) Glucose is broken down without oxygen to produce lactic acid
B) Glucose is broken down using oxygen to release a large yield of ATP
C) Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm
D) Glucose is converted to ATP only in the cytoplasm
practice_questions.marks: B) Glucose is broken down using oxygen to release a large yield of ATP [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (one mark each):
• Aerobic requires oxygen; anaerobic does not [1 mark]
• Aerobic produces a much larger ATP yield [1 mark]
• Aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid (in animals) or ethanol and carbon dioxide (in yeast) [1 mark]
• Aerobic occurs mainly in mitochondria; anaerobic occurs in the cytoplasm [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to lactic acid in the body after a period of intense exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: After exercise, breathing and heart rate remain elevated (oxygen debt) [1 mark]; extra oxygen is used by the liver to break down lactic acid [1 mark]; lactic acid is converted back to glucose [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the above points.
Developing: States that breathing rate stays high but does not link to lactic acid removal.
Emerging: Vague reference to lactic acid causing tiredness.

practice_questions.text:
A student measures their breathing rate during rest, moderate exercise and intense exercise. The results show breathing rate is much higher during intense exercise and remains elevated for several minutes afterwards.
Explain why breathing rate stays elevated after intense exercise stops.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During intense exercise, oxygen supply cannot meet demand so anaerobic respiration occurs [1 mark]; lactic acid accumulates in muscles [1 mark]; after exercise, extra oxygen is needed to convert lactic acid back to glucose (oxygen debt) [1 mark]; breathing rate stays elevated to supply this extra oxygen until the debt is repaid [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: Links higher breathing to removing lactic acid but lacks mechanistic detail.
Emerging: States breathing rate stays high without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. Use your knowledge of aerobic respiration in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Muscle cells contract frequently and require large amounts of ATP [1 mark]; aerobic respiration, which produces the most ATP, occurs in mitochondria [1 mark]; more mitochondria means more sites for aerobic respiration and more ATP can be produced to meet the high energy demand [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the above points clearly linked.
Developing: States muscles need more energy but does not connect to mitochondria number.
Emerging: Identifies that muscles need energy.

practice_questions.text: Compare the products and ATP yield of aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans. Explain the advantage of each type of respiration in different situations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; large ATP yield; used during rest or sustained moderate exercise when oxygen is available [up to 3 marks].
Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid; small ATP yield; used during intense exercise when oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough [up to 2 marks].
Evaluation: Each type has an advantage in its context — aerobic is efficient for sustained activity; anaerobic allows cells to keep working temporarily when oxygen is limiting [1 mark].
Secure: Both types described with correct products; advantage addressed for at least one.
Developing: One type described correctly.
Emerging: Vague reference to oxygen being needed for one type.

practice_questions.text: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy required, accept above or below the arrow).
1 mark: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (allow light energy notation).

practice_questions.text: A student grows two identical tomato plants. Plant A is grown in a greenhouse with increased CO₂ concentration; Plant B is grown in a greenhouse with normal CO₂ concentration. Both greenhouses have the same temperature and light intensity. Predict and explain the difference in growth rate between the two plants.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Plant A grows faster [1]; CO₂ is a reactant in photosynthesis, so a higher concentration increases the rate of carbon fixation [1]; more glucose is produced per unit time, providing more energy for respiration and more building blocks for growth [1].
Secure: States Plant A grows faster [1]; links to more CO₂ increasing the rate of photosynthesis [1].
Developing: States Plant A grows faster without a clear explanation.
Emerging: Identifies CO₂ without linking to growth.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis, including what happens above the optimum temperature.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: As temperature increases, enzyme and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently, increasing the rate [1]; above the optimum, the enzyme’s active site changes shape (denatures) permanently [1]; substrate can no longer bind, so the rate falls sharply [1].
Secure: Temperature increases rate up to optimum [1]; above optimum enzymes denature [1].
Developing: States rate increases with temperature, then falls.
Emerging: States temperature affects rate.

practice_questions.text: A gardener notices that her tomato plants have yellow-green leaves and stunted growth. Suggest which mineral ion is deficient and explain how the deficiency causes these symptoms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth because nitrates are needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins (and DNA) [1][1]; magnesium deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll [1][1]. (Accept either deficiency with full explanation for 4 marks.)
Secure: Correct deficiency identified [1]; mechanism linked to symptom [1].
Developing: Names a deficiency without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: States a mineral is missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student could use pondweed to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in a school laboratory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Place pondweed in a beaker of water with the lamp at a measured distance [1]; count oxygen bubbles per minute (or measure gas volume using a gas syringe) [1]; change the distance from the lamp to alter light intensity, keeping temperature and CO₂ concentration constant [1]; repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean [1].
Secure: Uses distance to change light intensity [1]; counts bubbles [1]; two further valid points.
Developing: Describes set-up and mentions bubbles, limited method detail.
Emerging: States pondweed is used without methodological detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why plants store excess glucose as starch rather than keeping it as glucose.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Starch is insoluble, so it does not lower the water potential of the cell (does not cause water to enter by osmosis), making it safe to store in large amounts without affecting cell turgor (accept: starch is compact and insoluble, suitable for storage).

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a DNA nucleotide.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: names three components correctly (sugar / phosphate / one of four named bases) and states they are joined to form the nucleotide. Secure: names two components correctly. Developing: names one component. Emerging: vague reference to DNA components without precision.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain the role of mRNA in protein synthesis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes mRNA as a copy of the gene made in the nucleus, travelling to the ribosome, where it is read in triplets to join amino acids in the correct order. Secure: includes mRNA travelling to ribosome and directing amino acid order, with one step missing or vague. Developing: states mRNA carries information from nucleus to ribosome but omits triplet reading or amino acid joining. Emerging: vague statement about mRNA being involved in protein making.

practice_questions.text: A student claims that because two people share the same genotype for height-related genes, they must be the same height. Evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: challenges the claim by explaining that phenotype depends on both genotype and environment; provides a relevant environmental factor (e.g. nutrition) that can modify height; notes that most characteristics depend on multiple genes interacting; reaches a clear conclusion that the claim is oversimplified. Secure: identifies the environment as a modifier and gives a relevant example, but reasoning on multiple genes or data quality is limited. Developing: states environment affects characteristics but explanation is vague. Emerging: asserts the claim is wrong without reasoned explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: genotype = combination of alleles (specific genes/genetic variants); phenotype = observable/expressed characteristics. Both defined clearly. Secure: one definition correct and precise, the other vague. Developing: one definition partially correct. Emerging: confuses the two terms or gives a single vague answer.

practice_questions.text: A cell in a leaf contains the same genome as a root cell in the same plant. Explain why the two cells have different structures and functions.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that both cells have the same genome (all genes present) but different genes are expressed in each cell type; gene expression is controlled by non-coding regulatory regions of DNA; the proteins produced differ, giving each cell its specific structure and function. Secure: states that different genes are switched on or off in each cell and links this to different proteins produced. Developing: states that cells do not use all their genes, but does not explain regulation or protein link. Emerging: vague answer about cells being different without genomic reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a genome can be used as a model, and identify one limitation of using the letter-code (A, T, C, G) to represent DNA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that the letter model represents base sequences in a simplified, readable form; correctly identifies a limitation, e.g. the model does not show the physical double-helix structure, or does not show how bases interact chemically; notes the model allows scientists to compare sequences and identify variants. Secure: identifies a valid use and a valid limitation, both reasonably explained. Developing: describes the model accurately but gives a weak or absent limitation. Emerging: describes the base letters without discussing modelling as a concept.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following statements correctly describes elements in the same group of the periodic table?
A) They have the same number of electron shells.
B) They have the same number of protons.
C) They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.
D) They all have the same atomic mass.
practice_questions.marks: C) They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'displacement reaction' in the context of Group 7 elements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A more reactive halogen (1) takes the place of a less reactive halogen in a compound / in solution (1).
Secure: Correct concept with one example.
Developing: Vague reference to replacement without specifying reactivity.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Explain why reactivity increases going down Group 1 (the alkali metals).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Going down the group, the outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus (1); there are more inner shells, increasing shielding of the outer electron from the nuclear attraction (1); therefore the outer electron is more easily lost, making the atom more reactive (1).
Secure: Two of the above three points with correct direction.
Developing: States outer electron is further away but does not explain shielding or ease of loss.
Emerging: Correct direction only.

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of transition metals with those of Group 1 metals. Give at least four differences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Transition metals have higher melting points than Group 1 metals (1); they are harder and denser (1); they are much less reactive (1); they form coloured compounds and can have variable oxidation states (1); they can act as catalysts (accept any four from this list).
Secure: Three differences correctly stated.
Developing: Two differences.
Emerging: One correct property.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Mendeleev's periodic table provides an example of how scientific models gain credibility.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic weight and identified patterns of similar properties (1); he left deliberate gaps where no known element fitted (1); he predicted the properties of these missing elements (1); when elements were discovered with properties matching those predictions (e.g. gallium and germanium), the model was confirmed (1); making testable predictions that are subsequently verified is a key way that a scientific model gains acceptance (1).
Secure: Four points with clear connection to model credibility.
Developing: Describes predictions and discovery but does not connect to scientific process.
Emerging: Names Mendeleev with limited development.

practice_questions.text: Chlorine water is added to separate solutions of potassium bromide and potassium iodide. Predict and explain what you would observe in each case.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Potassium bromide: solution turns orange/brown (1) because chlorine displaces bromine (1) as chlorine is more reactive than bromine (1). Potassium iodide: solution turns brown/dark (1) because chlorine displaces iodine (1) as chlorine is more reactive than iodine (1).
Secure: Both correct observations with correct displacement explanation.
Developing: One correct with explanation, one vague.
Emerging: One correct observation without explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between speed and velocity. Give an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only); velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
1 mark: valid example, e.g. a car travelling at 20 m/s north has the same speed as one travelling at 20 m/s south, but different velocities.

practice_questions.text: A sprinter accelerates from rest to 9 m/s in 1.5 s. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{9 - 0}{1.5} = 6\) m/s\(^2\)

1 mark for correct substitution.
1 mark for correct answer with unit (m/s\(^2\)).

practice_questions.text:
A velocity-time graph shows a straight line from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (10 s, 30 m/s), then a horizontal line from (10 s, 30 m/s) to (20 s, 30 m/s).
(a) Calculate the acceleration in the first 10 seconds.
(b) Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(a = \frac{30 - 0}{10} = 3\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark]

(b) Distance in first 10 s = area under triangle = \(\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 30 = 150\) m [1 mark]
Distance in next 10 s = area under rectangle = \(10 \times 30 = 300\) m [1 mark]
Total = 150 + 300 = 450 m [1 mark]

Common error: using \(v \times t\) for the first section instead of finding the area of a triangle.

practice_questions.text: A train enters a station at 25 m/s and decelerates uniformly to rest. The braking distance is 625 m. Calculate the deceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\):
\(0 = 25^2 + 2a \times 625\)
\(0 = 625 + 1250a\)
\(1250a = -625\)
\(a = -0.5\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 0.5 m/s\(^2\)) [4 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct substitution, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for answer + unit]

Note: time was not given — \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) is the appropriate equation.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you could use a ramp, trolley and light gate to investigate how acceleration depends on the resultant force. Identify the independent, dependent and one control variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: names equipment without linking to variables.
Secure:
- Independent variable: resultant force (varied by changing hanging mass on a pulley).
- Dependent variable: acceleration (measured from light gate timing data).
- Control variable: total mass of trolley + masses kept constant.
- Method: release trolley from rest; light gate records time for known-width card to pass through two gates; calculate speed at each gate; acceleration = change in speed ÷ time between gates (or use data logger). Repeat for different forces; plot acceleration vs force.

[1 mark: independent variable correctly identified with method; 1 mark: dependent variable correctly identified; 1 mark: valid control variable; 1 mark: clear method showing how acceleration is actually measured]

practice_questions.text: Scientists use mathematical models to predict the motion of moving objects. Explain, using the equations of motion as an example, how mathematical models in science can be useful and what their limitations might be.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states models are used to make predictions.
Secure: the equations of motion (e.g. \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)) are a simple mathematical model — they can predict the speed and position of an object if acceleration is known and constant; this has real applications in transport engineering and spacecraft design.
Limitations: the model assumes uniform (constant) acceleration — in reality, air resistance and engine force change as speed changes, so the model breaks down for objects accelerating over long distances or at high speeds.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that models are always tested against real measurements; when predictions match observations closely, the model is said to be valid, but a single clear discrepancy can expose a limitation and prompt model refinement (IaS3).

[1 mark: model can predict speed/position given initial conditions; 1 mark: real application; 1 mark: identifies assumption of uniform acceleration; 1 mark: explains when this breaks down; 1 mark: links to testing models against data / IaS3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Earth emits mainly infrared radiation rather than visible light.
practice_questions.marks: The Earth's surface is much cooler than the Sun [1]. Cooler objects emit radiation at longer wavelengths (lower principal frequency), so the Earth emits mainly infrared rather than visible light [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the greenhouse effect and explain how it keeps the Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
practice_questions.marks: Greenhouse gases (e.g. carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface [1]. They re-emit this radiation in all directions, including back towards the surface [1]. This reduces the rate at which the Earth loses energy to space, keeping the surface warmer [1].

practice_questions.text: Scientists use computer climate models to make predictions about future global temperatures. Explain how scientists use evidence to increase confidence in their climate model predictions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that models are tested against historical temperature records, ice-core data and satellite measurements; notes that a model that reproduces past climate accurately is more trustworthy for future predictions; explains that multiple independent groups building models that give consistent results increases confidence; distinguishes between uncertainty in magnitude and certainty about the direction of change; mentions peer review as part of the validation process.
Secure: Identifies at least two types of evidence used to test models and links model testing to confidence in predictions.
Developing: States that scientists compare model outputs to real data, without explaining the significance.
Emerging: Vague reference to scientists using data.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'Because climate scientists disagree about exact temperature predictions, we cannot be sure that global warming is happening.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Distinguishes clearly between uncertainty about magnitude (how much warming) and confidence about direction (that warming is occurring); explains that models contain simplifications and produce a range of predictions; argues that multiple independent lines of evidence (historical records, ice cores, satellite data, multiple model groups agreeing) all support the conclusion that warming is occurring; evaluates the student's statement as a misrepresentation of what scientific uncertainty means; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly explains that uncertainty in models does not undermine the overall conclusion; references at least two lines of evidence.
Developing: Acknowledges some uncertainty but also some evidence for warming, without weighing them effectively.
Emerging: Simply agrees or disagrees with the statement without using scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which human activities have increased the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) [1]; deforestation / burning forests [1]; cement manufacture [1]. One mark each.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a positive feedback loop in the context of climate change. Use the melting of Arctic sea ice as an example.
practice_questions.marks: A positive feedback loop is one where an initial change triggers further changes that amplify the original effect [1]. As temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice melts, exposing darker ocean water [1]. The ocean absorbs more solar radiation than ice, causing additional warming, which melts more ice — amplifying the original warming [1].

practice_questions.text: Balance the following equation: __ Mg + __ O<sub>2</sub> → __ MgO
practice_questions.marks: Award: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. Coefficients 2, 1, 2 or equivalent correct balanced equation.

practice_questions.text: Write the formula of calcium chloride, given that calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions and chloride is Cl<sup>−</sup>.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CaCl<sub>2</sub> written correctly (1) with explanation that 2 chloride ions balance the 2+ charge (1).
Secure: correct formula, no explanation.
Developing: attempts to balance charges but formula incorrect.
Emerging: formula given without reference to charges.

practice_questions.text: The equation for the decomposition of copper carbonate is: CuCO<sub>3</sub> → CuO + CO<sub>2</sub>. If 62 g of CuCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes, calculate the mass of CuO produced. (M<sub>r</sub>: CuCO<sub>3</sub> = 124, CuO = 80.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: moles of CuCO<sub>3</sub> = 62 ÷ 124 = 0.5 mol (1); mole ratio 1:1 so 0.5 mol CuO (1); mass = 0.5 × 80 = 40 g (1).
Secure: method correct, arithmetic error in one step.
Developing: moles calculated but ratio step missing.
Emerging: formula correct but no mole calculation.

practice_questions.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3\). Compare the mass of ammonia produced from 28 g of nitrogen versus 6 g of hydrogen (assume the other reactant is in excess). (M<sub>r</sub>: N<sub>2</sub> = 28, H<sub>2</sub> = 2, NH<sub>3</sub> = 17.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: from N<sub>2</sub>: moles = 28 ÷ 28 = 1 mol; ratio 1:2 so 2 mol NH<sub>3</sub>; mass = 34 g (2); from H<sub>2</sub>: moles = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 mol; ratio 3:2 so 2 mol NH<sub>3</sub>; mass = 34 g (2); both give 34 g — comparison stated.
Secure: both calculations correct, comparison not explicitly stated.
Developing: one calculation correct.
Emerging: moles calculated for one substance only.

practice_questions.text: Iron reacts with sulfuric acid according to: Fe + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → FeSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced from 0.4 mol of iron, and give the state symbols for all four substances. (M<sub>r</sub> of H<sub>2</sub> = 2.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mole ratio Fe:H<sub>2</sub> = 1:1 so 0.4 mol H<sub>2</sub> (1); mass = 0.4 × 2 = 0.8 g (1); correct state symbols Fe(s), H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq), FeSO<sub>4</sub>(aq), H<sub>2</sub>(g) (1).
Secure: mass correct, some state symbols wrong.
Developing: mass correct, state symbols not attempted.
Emerging: ratio identified but calculation incomplete.

practice_questions.text: A student is asked to balance and use the equation for the complete combustion of propane: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. First balance the equation. Then calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 22 g of propane burns completely. (M<sub>r</sub>: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> = 44, CO<sub>2</sub> = 44.) Explain each step of your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: balanced equation \(C_3H_8 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O\) (2); moles propane = 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol (1); ratio 1:3 so 1.5 mol CO<sub>2</sub> (1); mass = 1.5 × 44 = 66 g (1); each step clearly explained (1).
Secure: balanced equation and mass correct, limited explanation of steps.
Developing: equation balanced but ratio applied incorrectly.
Emerging: equation partially balanced, mass calculation not reached.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a stem cell?
A) A specialised cell that can only carry out one function
B) An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become different cell types
C) A cell found only in the nervous system
D) A cell that has stopped dividing permanently
practice_questions.marks: B) An undifferentiated cell that can divide and become different cell types [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells.
practice_questions.marks: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can become almost any cell type) [1 mark]; adult stem cells are more restricted and can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Auxin is produced at the shoot tip and migrates to the shaded side [1 mark]; higher auxin concentration causes cells on the shaded side to elongate more [1 mark]; unequal growth causes the shoot to bend towards the light [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three mechanistic steps above.
Developing: States auxin moves to one side but does not explain cell elongation.
Emerging: States the shoot bends without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: A patient with type 1 diabetes may benefit from stem cell therapy in the future. Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells in developing this therapy. Consider both the scientific potential and the ethical concerns.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Benefits: embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and could be directed to become insulin-producing (beta) cells [1 mark]; could restore normal blood glucose control without the need for daily insulin injections [1 mark]; embryos used are typically surplus from IVF treatment [1 mark].
Risks/ethical concerns: embryos are potential human lives and using them raises ethical objections [1 mark]; risk of immune rejection of transplanted cells [1 mark]; stem cells may divide uncontrollably (cancer risk) [1 mark].
Conclusion: A balanced statement weighing scientific potential against ethical concerns.
Secure: Both benefits and concerns addressed; conclusion present.
Developing: One side only addressed.
Emerging: Vague reference to stem cells being useful or controversial.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a higher concentration of auxin inhibits root growth but promotes shoot growth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots [1 mark]; in roots, high auxin inhibits cell elongation, so the side with more auxin grows less and the root bends towards higher auxin (downward) [1 mark]; in shoots, the same high concentration promotes cell elongation [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States roots and shoots respond differently but without mechanistic detail.
Emerging: Vague statement about auxin and growth.

practice_questions.text:
A scientist is studying cells from bone marrow and compares them with cells from a 3-day-old embryo.
Compare the differentiation potential of these two types of stem cell, and suggest one medical application of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can become almost any cell type); bone marrow stem cells are multipotent (can only become blood cells and related types) [1 mark each for contrast, 2 marks total]; embryonic: could be used to grow replacement insulin-producing cells or nerve cells [1 mark]; bone marrow: used in bone marrow transplants to restore blood cell production in leukaemia patients [1 mark].
Secure: Contrast stated plus one application.
Developing: One stem cell type described.
Emerging: Vague reference to stem cells treating disease.

practice_questions.text: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Show, using a Punnett square, the possible genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, including the ratio of phenotypes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: correct Punnett square with parent gametes labelled (T and t on each axis); all four offspring genotypes correct (TT, Tt, Tt, tt); phenotype ratio stated as 3 tall : 1 dwarf; probability of dwarf offspring stated as 1 in 4 or 25%. Secure: correct Punnett square and phenotype ratio; minor omission (e.g. probability not stated). Developing: Punnett square set up correctly but ratio or phenotype inference incomplete. Emerging: Punnett square attempted but genotypes incorrect or not linked to phenotypes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a dominant allele and a recessive allele.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: dominant is expressed when one or two copies are present; recessive is only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive). Secure: both concepts stated but one lacks precision (e.g. 'recessive needs two copies' without specifying homozygous). Developing: one concept correct and one absent. Emerging: vague answer about 'stronger' or 'weaker' genes without reference to copies.

practice_questions.text: Explain how biological sex is determined in humans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: states females are XX and males are XY; all eggs contain X but sperm carry either X or Y; sex is determined at fertilisation by which sperm (X or Y) fertilises the egg; probability of each sex is 1 in 2. Secure: correct sex chromosome notation and sperm carry X or Y; probability missing or minor error. Developing: sex chromosomes named correctly but fertilisation mechanism vague. Emerging: states males and females have different chromosomes but no further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Mendel crossed two heterozygous pea plants (Yy × Yy) and recorded 100 offspring. He observed 73 yellow seeds and 27 green seeds. Explain whether this data supports Mendel's model of inheritance, and evaluate the reliability of his data.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: calculates expected ratio from model (75 yellow : 25 green); notes the observed data is close to but not exactly 3:1; explains this is expected because probability applies to large samples but individual outcomes are random; evaluates reliability by noting sample size of 100 is reasonable but larger samples would reduce variation from expected; conclusion that data broadly supports the model. Secure: compares observed to expected ratio; discusses random variation; conclusion present but evaluation of reliability limited. Developing: calculates expected ratio and notes similarity to data, without discussing randomness. Emerging: notes data is close to expected but provides no reasoning about probability or sample size.

practice_questions.text: A person has the genotype Bb for a particular gene where B is dominant. State whether this person is homozygous or heterozygous, and predict whether the dominant or recessive phenotype is expressed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: heterozygous; dominant phenotype expressed (B is present). Both points required for the mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the scientific significance of Mendel's data with his explanatory theory. Why is it important to distinguish between the two?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clearly distinguishes data (observed counts of offspring phenotypes in defined crosses) from theory (hereditary factors in pairs, segregating into gametes); explains that data alone does not prove a theory but can support or challenge it; notes Mendel's theory was accepted because it correctly predicted data; mentions modern genetics extended the model using chromosomes and DNA; notes importance of this distinction for evaluating scientific claims (understanding that data is observation, theory is explanation). Secure: distinguishes data from theory; links to modern genetics; some evaluation of how models develop. Developing: states Mendel had data and a theory but does not clearly distinguish them or link to scientific reasoning. Emerging: describes Mendel's work without addressing the question's focus on data versus explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for efficiency.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy transferred [1 mark]. Accept: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.

practice_questions.text: A light bulb takes in 60 J of electrical energy each second and transfers 12 J as light. Calculate its efficiency and state how much energy is wasted each second.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.2 (or 20%) [1 mark]. Wasted energy = 60 − 12 = 48 J per second (48 W wasted as thermal energy) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how fitting a car engine with better lubrication improves its efficiency. Refer to energy stores in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts [1 mark]. Less energy is therefore transferred to the thermal store of the engine (wasted as heat) [1 mark]. So a greater fraction of the chemical energy from fuel is transferred usefully as kinetic energy, increasing efficiency [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that lubrication reduces friction and improves efficiency but does not link to energy stores.

practice_questions.text: A wind turbine has a power input of 8,000 W from the wind and a useful electrical power output of 2,800 W. Calculate the efficiency. Compare this with a coal-fired power station that operates at 35% efficiency. Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using the wind turbine instead.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 2800 ÷ 8000 = 0.35 (35%) [1 mark]. Both operate at the same efficiency [1 mark]. Advantage: wind is a renewable resource so will not run out; no carbon dioxide emissions [1 mark — any valid advantage]. Disadvantage: wind turbines only generate when wind is blowing (intermittent supply); output depends on wind speed [1 mark — any valid disadvantage].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct efficiency, correct comparison, one advantage and one disadvantage.
Developing: Correct efficiency but comparison or advantage/disadvantage incomplete.

practice_questions.text: A device has a total energy input of 500 J. Its Sankey diagram shows two output arrows: a useful output of 350 J and a wasted output. Calculate the efficiency of the device.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70 (or 70%) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'improving the efficiency of energy devices is the most important step we can take to address energy resource depletion.' Use your knowledge of efficiency and energy resources to argue both for and against this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for — higher efficiency means less total energy input is needed for the same useful output, so non-renewable resources last longer; uses efficiency equation to show that higher efficiency = less wasted energy; applies to specific examples (LEDs vs filament bulbs, electric motors vs combustion engines). Argues against — even a perfectly efficient device still uses an energy resource; switching to renewable sources removes dependence on depletable resources entirely; demand management and lifestyle changes may be equally important. Reaches a justified conclusion: improving efficiency is important but insufficient on its own.
Secure: Presents arguments on both sides with some reference to efficiency or energy resources.
Developing: Identifies efficiency as relevant but gives one-sided answer.
Emerging: Simple assertion without use of physics concepts.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'heterozygous'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Having two different alleles of a gene (e.g. Bb).
Secure: Two different versions of the gene / allele.
Developing: One dominant and one recessive — credit if linked to alleles.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: In guinea pigs, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant over the allele for white fur (b). Two heterozygous guinea pigs are crossed. Construct a Punnett square and state the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett square correctly drawn with parental gametes B and b along top and side (1 mark). Grid filled correctly: BB, Bb, Bb, bb (1 mark). Phenotype ratio stated as 3 black : 1 white (1 mark).
