Secure: Correct Punnett square and ratio but genotype and phenotype ratio confused.
Developing: Grid attempted but one or more cells incorrect; ratio stated.
Emerging: Parental genotypes written but no grid drawn.

practice_questions.text: A heterozygous guinea pig (Bb) is crossed with a homozygous recessive guinea pig (bb). Describe the expected genotype ratio and calculate the probability (as a percentage) that an offspring will show the dominant phenotype.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett square giving Bb, Bb, bb, bb. Genotype ratio Bb : bb = 1 : 1 (1 mark). Dominant phenotype (Bb) occurs in 2 out of 4 cells = 50% probability (1 mark). Clear working shown (1 mark).
Secure: Correct ratio and probability but working not clearly shown.
Developing: Correct ratio but probability calculated incorrectly.
Emerging: Punnett square attempted with errors; ratio guessed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Punnett squares give expected rather than guaranteed outcomes. Use the term 'probability' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett squares predict the probability of each genotype based on random combination of gametes during fertilisation. Because fertilisation is a random process, actual outcomes may differ from the predicted ratio, especially if the sample size is small. The more offspring produced, the closer results are likely to match the predicted ratio. (Award marks for: probability/randomness of fertilisation [1], link to sample size [1], conclusion about actual vs expected [1].)
Secure: Randomness and probability explained, some reference to sample size.
Developing: States that actual results may differ but does not explain why.
Emerging: Brief or vague reference to chance.

practice_questions.text: A genetic disorder is caused by a recessive allele (d). A child is born with the disorder. Both parents appear unaffected. Suggest, with reasoning, the likely genotypes of both parents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Child must have genotype dd (two recessive alleles, one from each parent). Since parents are unaffected, they each show the dominant phenotype; they cannot be dd. For each parent to pass on a d allele without showing the disorder, they must be heterozygous (Dd) carriers. Conclusion: both parents are Dd. Punnett square (Dd × Dd) confirms dd offspring is possible (25% probability). [4 marks: child's genotype dd [1]; reason parents must be carriers [1]; both parent genotypes stated as Dd [1]; supporting Punnett square or probability [1].]
Secure: Parents identified as Dd with valid reasoning; minor error in probability statement.
Developing: Parents identified as carriers but reasoning incomplete.
Emerging: Attempt at reasoning with genotype errors.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of Punnett squares as models for predicting genetic outcomes. In your answer, refer to both the strengths and limitations of the model.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strengths: Punnett squares provide a clear, structured method for predicting expected genotype and phenotype ratios for single-gene crosses; they model the random nature of gamete combination and enable probability calculations; they are widely used in medicine to predict risk of inherited disorders; they connect to established genetic theory (Mendelian inheritance). Limitations: they only model single-gene inheritance; most real characteristics are controlled by many genes and are also influenced by the environment, so a Punnett square for height or skin colour would be inaccurate; results are theoretical probabilities, not guaranteed outcomes — small sample sizes may give very different ratios; the model assumes all gametes are equally viable and that fertilisation is completely random, which may not always hold true. Conclusion: a strong model for simple inheritance but not suitable for complex multi-gene traits or predicting outcomes for individual pregnancies. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Both strengths and limitations addressed with relevant examples; some evaluative language.
Developing: Strengths or limitations described but not evaluated; limited range of points.
Emerging: One relevant point with little development or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vaccination protects an individual from a communicable disease.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: vaccine contains safe form of the pathogen (dead/weakened/parts); stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies specific to the pathogen's antigens; memory cells are formed; if real pathogen encountered, rapid secondary response produces antibodies quickly before symptoms develop; individual is protected. Secure: three of four points present and linked. Developing: two points present; mechanism partially explained. Emerging: states vaccine prevents disease without explaining the immunological mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a large proportion of the population needs to be vaccinated for herd immunity to be effective.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: if enough people are immune, pathogen cannot find susceptible hosts to spread between; chains of transmission break before the pathogen reaches unvaccinated individuals; vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated are indirectly protected. Secure: links proportion vaccinated to reduced transmission and protection of vulnerable; one point vague. Developing: states more vaccinated = less spread without explaining mechanism. Emerging: vague statement about herd immunity without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A new rapid diagnostic test uses monoclonal antibodies to detect a bacterial antigen in a blood sample. Evaluate the advantages of this approach compared with traditional bacterial culture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: monoclonal antibodies are highly specific (only bind to the target antigen, reducing false positives); rapid result time compared to days needed for culture; can be used in a clinical setting without specialist microbiology lab; limitation: may only detect one specific pathogen so a negative result does not rule out other infections; traditional culture allows antibiotic sensitivity testing which the antibody test does not; overall evaluation — antibody test faster and highly specific but culture provides more information. Secure: advantages and at least one limitation clearly compared; conclusion present. Developing: advantages stated but limited comparison with culture; no real evaluation. Emerging: describes monoclonal antibodies without comparing to culture or evaluating.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the steps involved in producing monoclonal antibodies for use in a diagnostic test.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: antigen injected into an animal to stimulate immune response; antibody-producing cells taken from the animal; cells producing the correct antibody are selected; these cells are cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies all recognising the same antigen. Steps in order, all four present. Secure: three steps correct. Developing: two steps described; sequence not fully correct. Emerging: general reference to antibodies being produced without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: A parent is deciding whether to vaccinate their child against a common disease. The child is healthy and many children in the class are already vaccinated. Using ideas about risk, benefit and decision-making, discuss the factors the parent should consider.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefits of vaccination (protection for child, memory cells, rapid response if infected); risks of vaccine (minor side effects, rare adverse reactions); herd immunity argument (most classmates immune, so risk to unvaccinated child is currently lower); but if too many parents reason this way herd immunity breaks down and disease resurges; individual right to decide vs societal responsibility; role of evidence and expert guidance; balanced conclusion with reference to weighing probability of harm (disease) versus probability and severity of vaccine side effects. Secure: benefits and risks addressed; herd immunity logic included; some weighing and conclusion. Developing: benefits and risks listed without weighing; herd immunity mentioned but not developed. Emerging: one-sided answer focusing only on vaccine risks or only on benefits.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between the primary and secondary immune responses.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: primary is slower / takes several days to produce significant antibody levels; secondary is faster / antibodies produced almost immediately due to memory cells. Two clear differences stated. Secure: one difference fully explained and one partially. Developing: one difference correctly stated. Emerging: vague reference to body recognising pathogen again without specifying what differs.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an abiotic and a biotic factor. Give one example of each in a UK freshwater pond ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: abiotic = non-living physical/chemical factor (e.g. water temperature, pH, light intensity, dissolved oxygen).
1 mark: biotic = living component (e.g. predatory fish, competing algae, disease organisms, availability of invertebrate prey).

practice_questions.text: A food web in a UK meadow includes: grass → voles → kestrels; grass → rabbits → foxes; voles → foxes. A disease kills most of the rabbit population. Predict and explain the likely short-term effects on the kestrel and fox populations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fox population decreases because rabbits are a major prey source [1]; foxes may then eat more voles as an alternative prey [1]; vole population decreases due to increased fox predation [1]; with fewer voles, kestrel population could decrease [1]; accept alternative valid chain with reasoning; conclusion weighs the net effect on each species [1].
Secure: Correct direction for at least two populations with valid reasons [1][1]; one further valid linked effect.
Developing: Identifies one population change without clear reasoning.
Emerging: States a population changes without linking it to the food web.

practice_questions.text: What is a niche? Explain why two species that occupy identical niches cannot coexist in the same ecosystem long-term.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A niche is the full role of a species in its ecosystem (what it eats, where, when, how it interacts) [1]; two species occupying the same niche compete for identical resources [1]; the more competitive species will out-compete the other, which is displaced or goes locally extinct [1].
Secure: Defines niche [1]; explains competition leads to one species winning [1].
Developing: States they compete without explaining the outcome.
Emerging: States they need the same things.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between mutualism and parasitism, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mutualism: both species benefit [1]; example e.g. clownfish and sea anemone, or bee pollination of flowers [1]; Parasitism: parasite benefits, host is harmed [1]; example e.g. flea and mammal, or tapeworm in gut [1].
Secure: Correct definition of each with one valid example each.
Developing: One type correctly defined with example.
Emerging: Names one type without definition.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the carrying capacity of an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The maximum population size that an environment can sustainably support, determined by the availability of resources such as food, water and space.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that removing a top predator from an ecosystem will always result in an increase in the prey population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Initial increase in prey likely as predation pressure removed [1]; however, prey may over-consume their own food source (plants/lower consumers), reducing its availability [1]; increased intraspecific competition among prey as numbers grow [1]; disease spread may increase at high density [1]; other predators may fill the vacant niche [1]; balanced conclusion: short-term increase likely, long-term outcome depends on other limiting factors [1].
Secure: Short-term increase explained [1]; at least two qualifying factors identified.
Developing: States prey increases without qualification.
Emerging: Agrees or disagrees with no scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of an endothermic reaction?
A) Combustion of natural gas
B) Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide
C) Thermal decomposition of copper carbonate
D) Rusting of iron
practice_questions.marks: C) Thermal decomposition of copper carbonate [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'activation energy'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The minimum energy (1) that reacting particles must have for a reaction to occur / to overcome the energy barrier (1).
Secure: States minimum energy needed but no reference to particles or reaction occurring.
Developing: Vague reference to energy needed to start a reaction.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A student mixes citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate in a test tube. The test tube feels cold to the touch. Describe and explain what type of reaction has taken place.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The reaction is endothermic (1). Energy is absorbed from the surroundings (the test tube and the student's hand) (1). This causes the temperature of the surroundings to fall, which is why the test tube feels cold (1).
Secure: Identifies endothermic and gives one developed point.
Developing: Identifies endothermic with a simple explanation.
Emerging: States the tube is cold without explaining the energy transfer.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic energy profile diagram, with reference to the positions of reactants and products and the activation energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both have a peak representing activation energy (1). In exothermic: products are at a lower energy level than reactants (1). In endothermic: products are at a higher energy level than reactants (1). The activation energy arrow must run from the reactant level to the peak of the curve in both cases (1).
Secure: Correct on relative positions of reactants/products plus one other point.
Developing: Distinguishes exo from endo but does not address activation energy correctly.
Emerging: Vague description of diagrams.

practice_questions.text: Explain in terms of bond breaking and bond making why an exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Breaking bonds in reactants requires energy (1); forming bonds in products releases energy (1); in exothermic reactions, more energy is released making new bonds than is needed to break existing bonds, so there is an overall release of energy to the surroundings (1).
Secure: Both bond-breaking and bond-making addressed with a conclusion.
Developing: States bond breaking requires energy or bond making releases energy, not both.
Emerging: Vague reference to bonds without explaining energy direction.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of a polystyrene cup in a laboratory investigation to measure the energy change in a chemical reaction. Include in your answer what a student should measure and how the energy change should be determined.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies polystyrene as a good thermal insulator, reducing heat loss to the surroundings and improving accuracy (1); student measures the temperature of the solution before and after the reaction (1); the temperature change (ΔT) indicates whether the reaction is exo- or endothermic (1); limitations: some heat loss still occurs even with insulation (1); a lid would further reduce heat loss (1); the method does not account for heat absorbed by the equipment itself, so a correction factor or calorimetry constant would improve accuracy (1).
Secure: Four points with logical organisation.
Developing: Two or three points, some structure.
Emerging: Names polystyrene and temperature measurement only.

practice_questions.text:
During electrolysis, where do positive ions (cations) move?
A) To the anode
B) To the cathode
C) They do not move
D) Away from both electrodes
practice_questions.marks: B) To the cathode [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'electrolyte' and explain why it must be molten or dissolved in water for electrolysis to work.
practice_questions.marks: An electrolyte is an ionic compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved [1]; it must be molten or dissolved so that the ions are free to move and carry charge [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at the cathode and at the anode when molten sodium chloride (NaCl) is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Cathode: Na⁺ ions attracted to cathode [1]; gain electrons to form sodium metal [1]. Anode: Cl⁻ ions attracted to anode; lose electrons to form chlorine gas (Cl₂) [1].

practice_questions.text:
A student electrolyses copper sulfate solution using carbon electrodes.
(a) Predict and explain the product at the cathode.
(b) Predict and explain the product at the anode.
Explain your reasoning for each electrode.
practice_questions.marks: (a) Copper is deposited at the cathode [1] because copper is less reactive than hydrogen so Cu²⁺ ions are preferentially discharged [1]. (b) Oxygen is produced at the anode [1] because no halide ions are present so OH⁻ ions are discharged instead [1].

practice_questions.text:
Write the half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and anode during the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃).
(Higher Tier)
For each half-equation, state whether oxidation or reduction occurs and explain why.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al [1]; reduction — gain of electrons [1]. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ [1]; oxidation — loss of electrons [1]; electrons balance (6 in each when scaled: 2Al³⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Al and 3O²⁻ → 3/2 O₂ + 6e⁻) [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: correct cathode half-equation and states reduction.

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain why aluminium extraction by electrolysis is more expensive than extracting iron by reduction with carbon in a blast furnace. In your answer, refer to the role of cryolite, the behaviour of the carbon anodes, and the energy requirements of each process.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series so cannot be extracted with carbon [1]; electrolysis requires large, continuous amounts of electrical energy [1]; aluminium oxide has a very high melting point [1]; cryolite is used to dissolve Al₂O₃ and lower the operating temperature, reducing energy costs somewhat [1]; carbon anodes burn away because oxygen reacts with them at high temperature [1]; they must be replaced regularly, adding to maintenance and material costs [1]. Secure: four well-explained points. Developing: identifies electrolysis used and mentions high energy cost.

practice_questions.text: Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
practice_questions.marks: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O (1 mark). State symbols not required unless the question asks for them.

practice_questions.text: Name the salt produced when zinc reacts with sulfuric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Zinc sulfate (1 mark). No mark for zinc sulfide (wrong anion) or zinc chloride (wrong acid).

practice_questions.text: A student adds hydrochloric acid to sodium hydroxide solution. Describe how they would use an indicator to determine when neutralisation is complete.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: add a few drops of a suitable indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange) to the alkali (1); add acid from the burette slowly, swirling the flask (1); the end point is when the indicator changes colour permanently and does not return to the original colour (1). Secure: three steps. Developing: indicator named and colour change described, method incomplete. Emerging: one step.

practice_questions.text: Outline a method to make a pure, dry sample of magnesium chloride from magnesium oxide and hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: add excess magnesium oxide to warm hydrochloric acid and stir (1); filter to remove excess magnesium oxide (1); heat the filtrate to evaporate water until crystals begin to form, then leave to cool (1); filter the crystals and dry them at low temperature (1). Secure: all four stages. Developing: three stages. Emerging: two stages.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out a titration using sodium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid. Their results give three titres: 24.30 cm³, 24.25 cm³, 24.80 cm³. Calculate the mean titre the student should use.
practice_questions.marks: Identifies that 24.80 cm³ is anomalous/not concordant with the others and excludes it (1); mean = (24.30 + 24.25) ÷ 2 = 24.28 cm³ (1). Mastering: anomaly identified and mean correct. Secure: correct answer. Developing: calculates mean of all three without excluding anomaly. Emerging: no anomaly identified.

practice_questions.text: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are both acids, but at the same concentration hydrochloric acid has a lower pH. Explain why, and what this tells us about their degree of ionisation in water.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and fully ionises in water, producing the maximum number of H⁺ ions (1); ethanoic acid is a weak acid that only partially ionises — an equilibrium is established (1); more H⁺ ions in the hydrochloric acid solution gives a lower pH at the same concentration (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of bacteria responsible for converting ammonium ions into nitrate ions in the soil.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Nitrifying bacteria.

practice_questions.text: Explain why burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations more than burning wood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fossil fuels contain carbon that has been locked underground for millions of years [1]; burning them releases this ancient carbon into the active cycle [1]; whereas wood contains recently fixed carbon that was recently part of the atmosphere [1].
Secure: States fossil fuels contain old carbon [1]; burning releases it to atmosphere [1].
Developing: States burning fossil fuels releases CO₂.
Emerging: States fossil fuels cause climate change.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of eutrophication, beginning with excess nitrate entering a river.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Excess nitrate causes rapid algal growth (algal bloom) [1]; algae block light and aquatic plants die; decomposers break down the dead material using oxygen [1]; dissolved oxygen in the water falls, causing death of fish and other aerobic organisms [1].
Secure: Algal bloom [1]; oxygen depletion [1].
Developing: Algal bloom mentioned; limited further explanation.
Emerging: States too many nutrients are harmful.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of denitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle and state the conditions in which they are most active.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate ions back into nitrogen gas, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.
1 mark: They are most active in waterlogged (anaerobic) soils.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how deforestation affects both the carbon cycle and the water cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Carbon cycle: trees are a carbon store; when cut down and burned or left to decay, carbon is released as CO₂ [1]; fewer trees means less photosynthesis removing CO₂ from atmosphere [1]; net effect is increased atmospheric CO₂ [1]. Water cycle: fewer trees means less transpiration, reducing atmospheric moisture and local rainfall [1]; less interception of rainfall increases surface run-off and flood risk [1]; reduced infiltration reduces groundwater recharge [1].
Secure: Two valid carbon effects [1][1]; two valid water effects [1][1].
Developing: One effect from each cycle.
Emerging: States deforestation is harmful without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules benefit both themselves and the leguminous plant they inhabit.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into ammonia or nitrate ions [1]; the plant can absorb these to make amino acids and proteins [1]; in return, the plant provides the bacteria with organic compounds (sugars from photosynthesis) for energy [1]; this is a mutualistic relationship because both species benefit [1].
Secure: Bacteria fix nitrogen [1]; plant provides sugar [1].
Developing: States both benefit without mechanism.
Emerging: Names nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes ionic bonding?
A) Sharing of electrons between two non-metal atoms
B) Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
C) Delocalised electrons moving freely between metal ions
D) Attraction between molecules caused by weak intermolecular forces
practice_questions.marks: B) Transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'delocalised electron' in a metal.
practice_questions.marks: An electron that has left its parent atom [1] and is free to move throughout the metal structure / is not associated with any particular atom [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a dot-and-cross diagram shows the formation of magnesium oxide (MgO) by ionic bonding.
practice_questions.marks: Draw outer-shell electrons of Mg (2) and O (6) [1]; show transfer of 2 electrons from Mg to O [1]; draw resulting ions with charges Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ in square brackets with a full outer shell of 8 electrons on oxygen [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point but does not conduct electricity when solid, yet conducts when dissolved in water.
Use your knowledge of ionic bonding in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: High melting point: strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in all directions [1] require a large amount of energy to overcome [1]. Does not conduct when solid: ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move [1]. Conducts when dissolved: ions are free to move and carry charge through the solution [1].

practice_questions.text: A student states that 'aluminium rusts in air, just like iron.' Explain why this statement is incorrect, and describe what actually happens to aluminium when it is exposed to air.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies that rust is specifically an iron compound (iron(III) oxide) [1]; explains aluminium reacts with oxygen but forms a thin oxide layer (Al₂O₃) [1]; this layer is tightly bonded and impermeable, preventing further oxidation [1]; contrasts with iron's flaky, porous rust layer that allows continued attack [1]; concludes that aluminium appears unreactive in air because of this self-sealing protection [1]. Secure: first three points. Developing: two points with partial explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare ionic bonding and metallic bonding in terms of the particles involved, the nature of the attractive force, and the electrical conductivity of each type of substance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ionic — metal cations and non-metal anions [1], held by electrostatic attraction between opposite charges in a giant lattice [1], conducts only when molten or dissolved (ions free to move) [1]. Metallic — positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons [1], held by electrostatic attraction between ions and electron sea [1], conducts in all states because delocalised electrons are always free to move [1]. Secure: four points with correct reasoning. Developing: three points.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
practice_questions.marks:
\(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1500 \times 400 = 300{,}000\) J (300 kJ)

1 mark for correct substitution into \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).
1 mark for correct answer with unit (J or kJ).

Common error: forgetting the \(\frac{1}{2}\) factor, giving 600,000 J.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the relationship between force, change in momentum and time, why crumple zones at the front of a car reduce the risk of injury in a collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states crumple zones reduce the force.
Secure: crumple zone deforms during the collision, increasing the time over which momentum changes (\(\Delta t\) increases); since \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\) and momentum change is the same, a greater \(\Delta t\) means a smaller average force on the occupants.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that this reduces peak deceleration and therefore peak force; links to why the crumple zone design is at the front/rear (passenger compartment is rigid to protect occupants). Correctly rejects the explanation that crumple zones “absorb force.”

[1 mark: crumple zone extends collision time; 1 mark: same \(\Delta p\) over longer \(\Delta t\) means smaller \(F\) using \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\); 1 mark: therefore force on passengers is reduced → injury risk lower]

practice_questions.text:
A cyclist of mass 75 kg (including bicycle) is travelling at 8 m/s.
(a) Calculate the momentum of the cyclist.
(b) The cyclist brakes to a stop in 4 s. Calculate the average braking force.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(p = mv = 75 \times 8 = 600\) kg m/s [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) Change in momentum \(\Delta p = 600 - 0 = 600\) kg m/s
\(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{600}{4} = 150\) N [2 marks: 1 for identifying \(\Delta p\), 1 for correct force with unit]

Alternatively via \(F = ma\): \(a = (0 - 8)/4 = -2\) m/s\(^2\); \(F = 75 \times 2 = 150\) N ✓ [1 mark for either valid method]

practice_questions.text:
A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 8 m. Calculate:
(a) The gravitational potential energy at the top.
(b) The speed of the ball just before it hits the ground. (Assume no air resistance; g = 10 N/kg.)
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(E_{gpe} = mgh = 0.5 \times 10 \times 8 = 40\) J [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) By conservation of energy: \(E_k = 40\) J
\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 40 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow 0.25v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow v^2 = 160 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{160} \approx 12.6\) m/s [3 marks: 1 for equating GPE to KE, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain the factors that affect both the thinking distance and the braking distance of a vehicle, and discuss how Newton's laws of motion have led to improvements in road safety through the design of safety features.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: lists some factors without explanation.
Developing: identifies thinking distance factors (reaction time, speed, alcohol/drugs/distractions) and braking distance factors (speed, road surface, tyre/brake condition, mass) with brief explanation.
Secure: as Developing, plus explains the physics — braking distance ∝ v² because KE = ½mv²; stopping requires KE to be removed by work done by braking force (W = Fd); larger KE needs more braking distance; also explains crumple zones, seatbelts or airbags using the impulse/momentum principle (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)).
Mastering: as Secure, plus evaluates the trade-off — increasing collision time reduces force but requires the car to crumple (permanent deformation is the cost); risk-benefit framing: society accepts the cost of replacing the crumple zone because the benefit (reduced injury) far outweighs it; links to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis.

[2 marks: thinking distance factors correctly explained; 2 marks: braking distance factors correctly explained with \(v^2\) link; 1 mark: safety feature explained using impulse/momentum; 1 mark: risk-benefit or Newton's law evaluation]

practice_questions.text: A 2000 kg lorry travelling at 15 m/s collides with and attaches to a stationary 500 kg car. Calculate the velocity of the combined vehicles immediately after the collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Use conservation of momentum:
Momentum before = \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (2000 \times 15) + (500 \times 0) = 30{,}000\) kg m/s [1 mark]
Momentum after = \((m_1 + m_2)v = 2500v\) [1 mark]
\(2500v = 30{,}000 \Rightarrow v = \frac{30{,}000}{2500} = 12\) m/s [2 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct answer with unit]

Common error: not adding masses after attachment, or only using one object's momentum.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'random sample' in an ecological investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sample where every individual / location has an equal chance of being chosen, selected without bias (e.g. using random numbers / random coordinates).
Secure: Every location has an equal chance of being selected.
Developing: Reference to avoiding bias without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: A student records the number of earthworms in six 1 m² quadrats: 4, 7, 5, 6, 4, 8. Calculate the mean number of earthworms per quadrat. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sum = 4+7+5+6+4+8 = 34. Mean = 34 ÷ 6 = 5.67 (to 2 decimal places) or 5.7 earthworms per quadrat. (Both marks: correct sum and division shown [1] + correct answer [1].)
Secure: Method correct but arithmetic error in sum; or correct answer without working shown.
Developing: Addition attempted but division step missing or incorrect.
Emerging: One or two values summed with no clear method.

practice_questions.text: Using your answer from above, estimate the total number of earthworms in a 300 m² garden. The quadrats used are 1 m² each. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Number of quadrat-sized units in the garden = 300 ÷ 1 = 300. Estimated population = mean × 300 = 5.67 × 300 = 1,701 (or 5.7 × 300 = 1,710). (1 mark for method; 1 mark for correct calculation consistent with mean used.)
Secure: Correct method with minor arithmetic error; units used correctly.
Developing: Mean multiplied by 300 without justification; follow-through mark applied.
Emerging: Number of quadrats not considered.

practice_questions.text: In a woodland, the population of a bird species was 350 in Year 1. By Year 4, the population had risen to 427. Calculate the percentage change. Give your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Percentage change = (427 − 350) ÷ 350 × 100 = 77 ÷ 350 × 100 = 22.0% increase. (3 marks: correct formula [1]; correct substitution and calculation [1]; correct rounding and unit/direction stated [1].)
Secure: Formula correct and calculation attempted; answer not rounded or direction not stated.
Developing: (427 − 350) calculated correctly but then divided by 427 (using new value); or formula not shown.
Emerging: Difference calculated (77) but no percentage conversion.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates dandelion abundance in a school field and a nearby car park. They use random quadrats in each location and record a mean of 12 dandelions per m² in the field and 2 per m² in the car park. Suggest two reasons why the number of dandelions is higher in the field.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two valid reasons with explanation, e.g.: (1) More light available in the field — fewer obstacles block sunlight, so dandelions can photosynthesise more effectively and grow more densely. (2) Greater soil depth and quality in the field — car park surfaces may have thin soil with fewer nutrients, reducing plant growth. (3) Less physical disturbance in the field — cars compacting car park ground may damage plants or make germination difficult. [2 marks per reason: 1 for suggestion, 1 for explanation using science.]
Secure: Two reasons suggested with partial explanation.
Developing: Two reasons stated without scientific explanation.
Emerging: One relevant reason stated.

practice_questions.text: A long-term study found that as the mean summer temperature increased in a region, the average abundance of a butterfly species in field surveys also increased. A researcher concludes that higher temperatures cause butterfly populations to increase. Evaluate this conclusion, referring to correlation, causation and alternative explanations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluation uses both sides. Supporting the conclusion: the data shows a positive correlation between temperature and butterfly abundance; warmer temperatures may increase butterfly survival, extend the breeding season, or improve host plant growth, providing biological plausibility. Challenging the conclusion: correlation does not prove causation; a third variable (e.g. increased plant growth due to warmer, wetter summers) could explain both the temperature rise and the butterfly increase independently; without a controlled experiment, it is not possible to establish a causal link; other factors such as habitat management, pesticide reduction, or migration patterns could contribute to the increase. Quality of evidence: sample size, number of years, and consistency across sites affect reliability. Conclusion: the correlation is consistent with a causal link but does not prove it; further controlled investigation is needed. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Correlation vs causation addressed; some alternative explanations given; attempted conclusion.
Developing: Correlation noted but alternative explanations limited or absent; limited evaluation.
Emerging: One relevant point about correlation or causation with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a greenhouse gas?
A) Nitrogen
B) Oxygen
C) Argon
D) Methane
practice_questions.marks: D) Methane [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how ice cores provide evidence about changes in atmospheric composition over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ice cores contain trapped air bubbles (1) from different time periods, with deeper ice corresponding to older atmosphere (1). Analysis of gas composition in these bubbles allows scientists to reconstruct the history of CO₂ concentration (and temperature) over hundreds of thousands of years (1).
Secure: Two points with some explanation.
Developing: Mentions trapped air or bubbles but no further development.
Emerging: Vague reference to ice providing evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why scientists use multiple independent lines of evidence when building a case for climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: No single measurement proves the case (1); when independent datasets from different sources tell the same story, this convergence increases confidence in the conclusion (1); if different methods with different potential errors all agree, it is unlikely they are all wrong in the same way (1).
Secure: Two points with logical connection.
Developing: States that more evidence is better without explaining why convergence matters.
Emerging: Vague answer.

practice_questions.text: Compare the natural greenhouse effect with the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both involve greenhouse gases absorbing infrared radiation emitted by the Earth (1). The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough to support life (1). The enhanced effect is caused by rising concentrations of CO₂ and methane from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and livestock farming (1). This traps more energy and raises global average temperatures beyond the natural baseline (1).
Secure: Natural vs enhanced clearly distinguished with two developed points.
Developing: One distinction made with partial development.
Emerging: Vague reference to more greenhouse gases.

practice_questions.text: A newspaper headline claims: 'Scientists cannot agree on climate change.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of how scientific evidence and models work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Challenges the claim — there is a strong scientific consensus that climate change is occurring and is linked to human greenhouse gas emissions (1). This consensus is based on convergence of multiple independent evidence sources (1). Uncertainty exists in the precise projections of future change, not in the fundamental conclusion (1). Uncertainty in a model does not mean disagreement among scientists about the direction of change (1). The distinction between reporting uncertainty in projections and claiming there is no consensus is important for public understanding of science (1).
Secure: Four points, logically connected.
Developing: Challenges claim with two supporting points.
Emerging: Challenges claim but minimal support.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the risks and benefits of reducing fossil fuel use as a response to climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits: reduces CO₂ emissions and slows further warming (1); reduces other pollutants such as particulates that harm health (1). Risks/costs: economic disruption to industries dependent on fossil fuels (1); transition costs for energy infrastructure (1). Weighing: the long-term projected consequences of continued warming (sea level rise, extreme weather, agricultural disruption) are likely to exceed the costs of transition (1); but the pace and distribution of costs and benefits is contested, and the most vulnerable communities often experience both the worst climate impacts and the greatest economic hardship from rapid transitions (1).
Secure: Both sides addressed with a weighing statement.
Developing: Lists risks and benefits without weighing.
Emerging: One-sided response.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by an exothermic reaction in terms of energy and temperature change.
practice_questions.marks: Award: a reaction in which energy is transferred to the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to rise. Accept equivalent correct wording.

practice_questions.text: In a bond energy calculation, what does a negative overall energy change tell you about the reaction?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: more energy is released making bonds than is required to break bonds (1), so the reaction is exothermic and transfers energy to surroundings (1).
Secure: states exothermic with partial explanation.
Developing: states exothermic but no explanation.
Emerging: incorrect interpretation of the sign.

practice_questions.text: The reaction of hydrogen with chlorine is: H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ/mol; Cl–Cl = 243 kJ/mol; H–Cl = 432 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: energy in = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ (1); energy out = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ (1); ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol, exothermic (1).
Secure: both totals correct, sign error or label missing.
Developing: one total correct, method partially shown.
Emerging: bond energies added without structure.

practice_questions.text: Sketch a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction and compare it with an endothermic reaction. On your diagram, label the activation energy and the overall energy change ΔH for each. Explain what activation energy represents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: exothermic profile with products below reactants (1); endothermic profile with products above reactants (1); activation energy labelled as the peak above reactants for both (1); explanation that activation energy is the minimum energy for a reaction to occur (1).
Secure: both profiles sketched, one label missing.
Developing: one profile correct with activation energy labelled.
Emerging: one profile attempted.

practice_questions.text: The combustion of methane is: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413; O=O = 498; C=O = 805; O–H = 463. Calculate the overall energy change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: bonds broken = (4 × 413) + (2 × 498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ (1); bonds made = (2 × 805) + (4 × 463) = 1610 + 1852 = 3462 kJ (1); ΔH = 2648 − 3462 = −814 kJ/mol, exothermic (1).
Secure: method correct, one counting error.
Developing: bonds broken calculated correctly only.
Emerging: equation for ΔH stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A student claims that all reactions with a high activation energy must be exothermic. Evaluate this claim. In your answer, refer to reaction profiles and bond energy calculations and give an example that supports or contradicts the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: correctly states that activation energy and overall energy change are independent quantities (2); explains that endothermic reactions can also have high activation energies (2); uses reaction profile evidence with reference to the position of reactants and products relative to the peak (1); gives a valid example or argues the point with bond energy logic (1).
Secure: claim correctly refuted, profiles referenced, one element incomplete.
Developing: claim refuted with some reasoning, no profile reference.
Emerging: limited or confused response.

practice_questions.text: A current of 2 A flows through a circuit for 30 seconds. Calculate the total charge that passes a point in the circuit.
Describe how the current and potential difference behave differently in a series circuit compared with a parallel circuit.
practice_questions.marks: In a series circuit, current is the same at every point but the potential difference is shared (split) across the components [1 mark]. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same as the supply, but the current splits between branches [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A 6 V battery is connected to three resistors in series: 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 2 Ω. Calculate the total resistance and the current in the circuit. Then calculate the potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor.
practice_questions.marks: Total resistance = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12 Ω [1 mark]. Current I = V ÷ R = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A [1 mark]. V across 6 Ω = 0.5 × 6 = 3 V [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Finds total resistance and current correctly but cannot calculate the pd across one resistor.

practice_questions.text: A lamp filament has a resistance of 240 Ω when hot. Calculate the current through the lamp when connected to a 12 V supply. Suggest why the resistance of the filament is much lower when the lamp is first switched on (before it heats up).
practice_questions.marks: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 240 = 0.05 A [1 mark]. When first switched on, the filament is cold [1 mark], so its resistance is lower [1 mark] because resistance of a metal increases with temperature (hotter metal atoms vibrate more, impeding charge flow more) [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct current and explains that cold filament has lower resistance due to temperature.
Developing: Correct current but does not explain resistance change in terms of temperature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why adding a resistor in parallel to an existing resistor decreases the total resistance of the circuit, even though you are adding more resistance.
practice_questions.marks: Adding a parallel branch provides an additional path for charge to flow [1 mark]. More paths mean more charge can flow per second for the same potential difference [1 mark], which is equivalent to a lower total resistance (since higher current at the same voltage means lower resistance by V = IR) [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that parallel adds a path and reduces resistance but does not link to current or V = IR.

practice_questions.text: A circuit contains a thermistor in series with a fixed resistor and a battery. The temperature of the thermistor rises. Evaluate what happens to the current in the circuit and the potential difference across the fixed resistor. Support your answer with reasoning from the relevant equations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises (correct property). Uses V = IR to reason: total resistance decreases, so for the same battery voltage, total current I = V/R_total increases. Applies the voltage-divider logic: because the fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged but current increases, the pd across the fixed resistor (V = I × R_fixed) increases. The pd across the thermistor decreases. Presents a coherent chain of reasoning.
Secure: Identifies thermistor resistance falls, current rises, pd across fixed resistor increases with correct use of V = IR.
Developing: Correctly identifies that thermistor resistance falls and current rises but does not address the pd across the fixed resistor.
Emerging: States thermistor resistance falls without further correct reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of CO₂ collected. In the first 30 seconds, 45 cm³ of gas is collected. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over this time. Include units.
practice_questions.marks: Rate = 45 cm³ ÷ 30 s = 1.5 cm³/s (1 mark for correct calculation; 1 mark for correct units of cm³/s). Common error: giving cm³/min by forgetting to convert. Mastering: correct answer with units. Secure: correct answer. Developing: correct division but wrong units. Emerging: formula not applied.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using collision theory, how increasing the temperature increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy (1); they move faster, so collisions are more frequent (1); a greater proportion of collisions have energy ≥ the activation energy, so more are successful (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points — frequency or proportion mentioned but not both. Emerging: 'particles collide more' without linking to kinetic energy or activation energy.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a catalyst and explain how it increases the rate of reaction without being used up.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in the overall reaction (1); it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (1); more collisions have sufficient energy to succeed, so the rate increases; the catalyst participates in the mechanism but is regenerated and not consumed overall (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: A reaction to make a drug compound produces 4.2 g of the desired product. The theoretical maximum yield is 6.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks: Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 (1 mark for formula); = (4.2 ÷ 6.0) × 100 (1 mark for substitution); = 70% (1 mark for answer); a percentage yield less than 100% could be due to incomplete reaction, product lost during transfer, or because the reaction is reversible (1 mark for reason). Mastering: all four. Secure: correct calculation and one reason. Developing: correct formula, arithmetic error. Emerging: formula stated only.

practice_questions.text: Hydrogen is manufactured by the reaction: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. The desired product is H₂. Calculate the atom economy for this reaction. (Mr: CH₄ = 16; H₂O = 18; H₂ = 2)
practice_questions.marks: Total Mr of desired product: 3 × 2 = 6 (1); total Mr of the reactants: 16 + 18 = 34 (1); atom economy = (6 ÷ 34) × 100 = 17.6% (allow 18%) (1); this is a low atom economy because CO is a by-product — most atom mass ends up as waste (1). Mastering: all four. Secure: correct calculation. Developing: formula applied but Mr sum incorrect. Emerging: formula stated only.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid using the disappearing cross method. Describe what they would measure and how they would calculate the rate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: place a conical flask over a piece of paper with a cross drawn on it (1); add sodium thiosulfate solution to the flask, then add hydrochloric acid and start a timer (1); record the time (in seconds) for the cross to disappear as sulfur precipitate forms (1); rate = 1 ÷ time — a shorter time means a faster rate (1). Secure: all four steps. Developing: three steps. Emerging: two steps.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes osmosis?
A) The movement of all molecules from high to low concentration using energy
B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
C) The movement of glucose against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins
D) The random movement of particles in all directions equally
practice_questions.marks: B) The net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which active transport differs from diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following:
• Active transport requires energy (from respiration); diffusion does not [1 mark]
• Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient; diffusion moves with the gradient [1 mark]
• Active transport uses carrier proteins in the membrane; diffusion does not require carrier proteins [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the alveoli are adapted to maximise the rate of gas exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large surface area provided by millions of alveoli [1 mark]; walls only one cell thick, minimising diffusion distance [1 mark]; rich capillary blood supply continuously removes oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide, maintaining steep concentration gradients [1 mark]; moist lining allows gases to dissolve before diffusing across the membrane [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four adaptations, each linked to diffusion rate.
Developing: One or two adaptations named without mechanistic link to diffusion.
Emerging: Vague reference to lungs being good at gas exchange.

practice_questions.text:
A student places a piece of potato in a concentrated salt solution and a second piece in pure water. After 30 minutes, the potato in salt solution has decreased in mass and the potato in water has increased in mass.
Explain these results using your knowledge of osmosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The salt solution is more concentrated than the potato cell contents [1 mark]; water moves out of the potato cells by osmosis (down the water potential gradient) into the salt solution [1 mark]; cells lose water, causing the potato to decrease in mass [1 mark]. In water, the solution is more dilute than the cell contents; water moves into the potato cells by osmosis, increasing their mass [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: Correct direction for one condition, without explanation in terms of water potential.
Emerging: States water moves in or out without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells require active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, whereas oxygen moves into blood by diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mineral ions are present in very low concentrations in the soil but in higher concentration inside the root hair cell [1 mark]; so minerals must be moved against the concentration gradient, which requires energy from respiration via active transport [1 mark]; oxygen, by contrast, is at higher concentration in the alveoli than in the blood, so it can move down its gradient by diffusion without energy [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States active transport requires energy without connecting to concentration gradient comparison.
Emerging: Names both processes but does not explain the distinction.

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages of the double circulatory system over a single circulatory system in meeting the high metabolic demands of mammals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit [1 mark]; the pulmonary circuit (heart to lungs) replenishes oxygen and removes CO₂ [1 mark]; the systemic circuit (heart to body) delivers oxygenated blood at high pressure to all tissues [1 mark]; separating the two circuits means blood is re-pressurised after passing through the lungs, so it reaches tissues at high pressure [1 mark]; high pressure means faster delivery of oxygen and glucose to active cells, sustaining high metabolic rates [1 mark]; a single circulation would have low pressure reaching the body after passing through the lungs, insufficient for active mammals [1 mark].
Secure: Four or five points clearly explained.
Developing: Describes the two circuits without explaining the pressure advantage.
Emerging: States blood goes to the lungs and body.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State the difference between a substitution mutation and an insertion mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: substitution = one base replaced by a different base (one codon affected); insertion = an extra base added, causing a frameshift so all subsequent triplets are altered. Secure: both types described but frameshift not mentioned. Developing: one type described correctly. Emerging: vague reference to bases changing without specifying type.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an insertion mutation in a gene is likely to have a more severe effect on the protein produced than a substitution mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: insertion causes a frameshift, shifting all subsequent triplets so every amino acid after the mutation point may be altered; substitution only changes one codon, so at most one amino acid changes; therefore insertion is more likely to disrupt protein function extensively. Secure: states frameshift disrupts subsequent codons; comparison to substitution included but mechanism less precise. Developing: states insertion changes more amino acids but does not explain frameshift mechanism. Emerging: vague statement that insertion is worse without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA can affect an organism's phenotype.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: non-coding regions regulate gene expression; mutation may increase or decrease expression of a particular gene; this changes the amount of protein produced, altering the phenotype, even though the protein's sequence is unchanged. Secure: links non-coding DNA to gene regulation and altered protein levels; mechanism slightly vague. Developing: states non-coding DNA affects whether a gene is switched on but does not link to phenotype change clearly. Emerging: states non-coding DNA does not code for protein without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: The sickle cell allele causes disease when two copies are inherited but provides some protection against malaria when one copy is inherited. Use this example to explain how the same mutation can be beneficial, neutral or harmful depending on context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains the allele is harmful in homozygous form (disease), protective in heterozygous form in malaria-endemic regions (benefit), and neutral in non-malaria regions; links to natural selection maintaining the allele where malaria is prevalent; draws the general principle that mutation consequence depends on genetic context and environment. Secure: explains both the harmful and beneficial aspects with reference to natural selection; general principle stated. Developing: describes the two outcomes but does not link to natural selection or general principle. Emerging: describes sickle cell disease correctly without addressing the context-dependence aspect.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A scientist studies a new gene variant in a population and finds it does not change the protein produced but is located in a regulatory region of DNA. Predict the likely effect on the organism, and justify your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: predicts the variant could alter gene expression (increase or decrease when/how much protein is made); notes the protein structure is unchanged so function is unchanged; concludes the effect on phenotype depends on whether expression changes are significant in context; may be neutral (expression change too small to matter) or potentially harmful/beneficial if expression is dramatically altered. Secure: predicts altered gene expression and links to phenotype; justification present but lacks nuance about context. Developing: states regulatory region affects expression; limited prediction of outcome. Emerging: vague answer about non-coding DNA not being important.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'genetic variant' and explain how genetic variants arise.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a genetic variant is a different version of a gene (or allele); genetic variants arise from mutations (changes to the base sequence of DNA). Both points needed for full credit.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the general formula for alkanes?
A) CₙH₂ₙ
B) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
C) CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
D) CₙHₙ
practice_questions.marks: B) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one difference in the products formed during complete combustion and incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel.
practice_questions.marks: Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide [1]; incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (and/or soot/carbon particles) instead [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of fractional distillation of crude oil and explain why different fractions are collected at different heights in the column.
practice_questions.marks: Crude oil is heated until it vaporises [1]; vapours rise up a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top [1]; different hydrocarbons condense at different heights because they have different boiling points — shorter chains have lower boiling points and condense nearer the top [1].

practice_questions.text: A sample of gas produced by cracking is bubbled through bromine water. The bromine water turns from orange to colourless. Explain what this result tells you about the gas produced, and write a possible cracking equation for decane (C₁₀H₂₂) to give this type of product alongside a shorter alkane.
practice_questions.marks: The result shows an alkene is present [1]; alkenes have a C=C double bond and are unsaturated [1]; they decolourise bromine water because bromine adds across the double bond [1]; e.g. C₁₀H₂₂ → C₄H₁₀ + C₆H₁₂ (or other valid balanced cracking equation giving an alkane + an alkene) [1].

practice_questions.text: Carbon monoxide is produced by the incomplete combustion of hydrocarbon fuels in car engines. Using your knowledge of the chemistry of carbon monoxide, explain why it is particularly hazardous to human health, and suggest one way this hazard is reduced in modern vehicles.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: CO is colourless and odourless so cannot be detected by the senses [1]; CO binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells [1]; prevents haemoglobin from carrying oxygen to cells/tissues [1]; can cause unconsciousness and death even at low concentrations [1]; modern cars fitted with catalytic converters that convert CO to CO₂: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂ [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: identifies CO as toxic and links it to haemoglobin.

practice_questions.text: Explain why crude oil must be processed before it can be used, and describe two ways in which the chemical industry converts crude oil fractions into products with greater economic value. Include the names of the processes and the types of hydrocarbons involved.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: crude oil is a mixture that cannot be used directly as it has no fixed boiling point / contains many different hydrocarbons [1]; fractional distillation separates it into fractions based on boiling point [1]; shorter-chain fractions such as petrol have greater demand but are in shorter supply [1]; cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes [1]; alkenes are valuable as monomers for making polymers (plastics) [1]; catalytic or steam cracking are the two named methods [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: explains fractional distillation only.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a ‘risk factor’ for a non-communicable disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A factor that increases the probability (or chance/likelihood) of developing a disease [1]; it does not guarantee that the disease will occur [1].
Secure: A factor that makes it more likely that someone will develop a disease, but does not mean they definitely will.
Developing: Something that raises the chance of disease.
Emerging: A thing that causes disease.

practice_questions.text: A study followed 10,000 adults for 20 years. It found that those who exercised fewer than 3 hours per week had a higher rate of cardiovascular disease than those who exercised more. A journalist reported: ‘Lack of exercise proves to cause heart disease.’ Explain why this conclusion is not fully supported by the evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the study shows a correlation, not causation [1]; explains that confounding variables (e.g. diet, smoking, genetic factors) may account for the difference [1]; notes that one study is insufficient — findings need to be replicated [1]; recognises a plausible mechanism would need to be established [1]; conclusion is clearly stated and evidence weighed [1].
Secure: States correlation vs causation [1]; identifies at least one confounding variable [1]; recognises replication is needed [1]; one further valid point.
Developing: Identifies correlation vs causation or one confounding variable, with limited further development.
Emerging: States the study is not proof, with no scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how both genetic and lifestyle risk factors can contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Genetic factors: some individuals inherit gene variants that increase insulin resistance or reduce insulin production [1]; Lifestyle factors: diet high in refined sugars / physical inactivity / obesity associated with insulin resistance [1]; interaction: genetic predisposition is amplified by lifestyle factors, compounding risk [1]; conclusion that neither acts in isolation [1].
Secure: One genetic factor [1] and one lifestyle factor [1] described; some reference to interaction.
Developing: Names risk factors without explaining their mechanisms.
Emerging: Names diabetes without linking to causes.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether high BMI is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Describe how she could design an epidemiological study to investigate this, including what data she would collect and how she would control for confounding variables.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large cohort study with participants at different BMI levels [1]; collect cardiovascular disease rates over time [1]; control for confounding variables e.g. smoking status, diet, exercise, age [1]; large sample size to ensure statistical reliability [1].
Secure: Describes collecting BMI and CVD data [1]; identifies need to control confounders [1]; two further valid points.
Developing: Basic method described; limited discussion of controls.
Emerging: States she would collect health data, with no further detail.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether the evidence that smoking causes lung cancer is stronger than evidence that eating saturated fat causes cardiovascular disease. Use your knowledge of how scientific evidence is evaluated.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Smoking-lung cancer: biological mechanism well-established (carcinogens in smoke damage DNA in lung cells) [1]; dose-response relationship clear [1]; consistent across many studies and populations [1]; Saturated fat-CVD: plausible mechanism (raises LDL, promotes atherosclerosis) [1]; but confounding variables harder to control in dietary studies [1]; reasoned conclusion on relative strength of evidence [1].
Secure: At least two valid points on each side; conclusion present.
Developing: Valid points on one side only.
Emerging: States one causes disease without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why an outlier in a dataset showing the relationship between alcohol consumption and liver disease should not automatically be removed from the analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Outliers are part of the real data; removing them without justification would bias the results / they may represent genuine variation in the population / their cause should be investigated first (accept any valid equivalent).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a correct statement about addition polymerisation?
A) A small molecule (e.g. water) is released at each bond
B) The monomer must have two functional groups
C) The monomer must contain a C=C double bond
D) The product is always a polyamide
practice_questions.marks: C) The monomer must contain a C=C double bond [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of bond formed when thermosetting polymers are heated and explain why they cannot be reshaped.
practice_questions.marks: Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links between chains [1]; these cross-links are permanent — heating cannot break them, so the chains cannot slide and the polymer cannot be reshaped [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. In your answer, refer to the monomers needed and whether any by-product is formed.
practice_questions.marks: Addition: monomers must contain a C=C double bond [1]; chains join with no by-product formed [1]. Condensation: monomers must have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH) [1]; a small molecule (usually water) is released at each bond formed [1]. (Max 3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: PET is used for fizzy drink bottles. Explain the structure of PET, name the type of monomers used to make it, and compare it with a thermosetting polymer in terms of thermal properties and recyclability.
practice_questions.marks: PET is a polyester [1]; made from a diol (ethylene glycol) and a dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) by condensation polymerisation [1]; it is a thermosoftening polymer — can be melted and reshaped / recycled [1]; unlike thermosetting polymers which have covalent cross-links and cannot soften or be recycled [1].

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer must choose between a thermosoftening polymer and a thermosetting polymer to make the handle of an electric saucepan that will reach temperatures above 100 °C. Evaluate which polymer is more appropriate, giving reasons for your choice and acknowledging a limitation of the chosen material.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: thermosetting is more appropriate for a saucepan handle [1]; because it has covalent cross-links that do not break at high temperatures [1]; it will not soften or deform when heated above 100 °C [1]; in contrast, a thermosoftening polymer would soften when heated, making it unsafe [1]; limitation: thermosetting cannot be recycled after use because the cross-links are permanent [1]; the manufacturer should consider this environmental disadvantage in a full life-cycle assessment [1]. Secure: four points with clear evaluation. Developing: correctly identifies thermosetting and gives one structural reason.

practice_questions.text: Write the repeat unit for poly(propene) and explain, in terms of bonding changes, how the monomer propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂) is converted to the polymer during addition polymerisation.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: correct repeat unit drawn or written: –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ– [1]; in addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in each propene monomer opens [1]; one bond of the double bond breaks [1]; the resulting reactive sites on adjacent monomers form new C–C single bonds [1]; building the chain; no atoms are lost — the empirical formula of the repeat unit is the same as the monomer [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: identifies C=C opens and chain forms.

practice_questions.text: A toaster draws a current of 4 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate its power rating.
A charge of 500 C flows through a lamp with a potential difference of 12 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred to the lamp.
practice_questions.marks: E = Q × V = 500 × 12 = 6,000 J [1 mark]. The energy is transferred to the lamp, mostly as light and thermal energy [1 mark — accept any statement correctly identifying the transfer].

practice_questions.text: A 1.5 kW hair dryer is used for 20 minutes each day for 30 days. Electricity costs 28p per kWh. Calculate the total cost of running the hair dryer over this period.
practice_questions.marks: Time = 20 min × 30 = 600 min = 10 hours [1 mark]. Energy = 1.5 kW × 10 h = 15 kWh [1 mark]. Cost = 15 × 28p = 420p = £4.20 [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly calculates energy in kWh but makes an error in the time conversion or the final cost.

practice_questions.text: A resistor has a resistance of 50 Ω and a current of 0.6 A flowing through it. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor. Then explain why this power appears as heating of the surroundings.
practice_questions.marks: P = I²R = 0.6² × 50 = 0.36 × 50 = 18 W [2 marks — 1 for correct squaring, 1 for final value]. As charge flows through the resistor, the moving charges collide with atoms in the material [1 mark], transferring energy to the thermal store of the resistor and then to the surroundings [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct power and explains charge–atom collisions causing heating.
Developing: Correct power calculation but explanation of heating is 'energy is lost' without mechanistic detail.

practice_questions.text: A step-up transformer in a power station increases voltage from 25,000 V to 400,000 V. The current in the primary coil is 800 A. Calculate the current in the secondary (high-voltage) coil.
practice_questions.marks: Using V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s: 25,000 × 800 = 400,000 × I_s [1 mark]. I_s = (25,000 × 800) ÷ 400,000 = 20,000,000 ÷ 400,000 = 50 A [1 mark]. State units: 50 A [1 mark — award final mark only if correct calculation shown].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Sets up the transformer equation correctly but makes an arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'the most effective way to reduce household electricity bills is to switch off appliances when not in use.' Use the equations for power, energy and cost to support or challenge this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses E = P × t to show that both power rating AND time of use contribute to energy consumed. Supports by calculating examples: a 2 kW heater left on for an hour costs more than a 100 W bulb left on for the same time. Challenges by noting that high-power appliances (ovens, showers, tumble dryers) may dominate the bill; switching off a phone charger (typically very low power) has negligible effect compared to reducing use of high-power devices. Suggests that reducing usage time of high-power appliances is most effective, not simply switching off standby devices. Uses cost = E × price to evaluate in financial terms. Reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly uses E = P × t; discusses at least two different power-rated appliances; addresses time of use.
Developing: Identifies that power and time both matter but does not use equations to quantify.
Emerging: Agrees with the claim without engaging with the physics.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between alpha particles and gamma rays.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two differences, 1 mark each:
- Alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons (helium nuclei); gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves (no mass or charge).
- Alpha particles are stopped by paper / a few cm of air; gamma rays require several cm of lead or metres of concrete.
- Alpha particles are strongly ionising; gamma rays are weakly ionising.
- Alpha emission reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2; gamma emission does not change mass number or atomic number.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive isotope has an activity of 6400 Bq. After 80 minutes, its activity has fallen to 400 Bq. Calculate the half-life.
practice_questions.marks:
Count halvings: 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 = 4 half-lives [1 mark]
4 half-lives = 80 minutes → half-life = \(80 / 4 = 20\) minutes [1 mark]

Common error: dividing 80 by 6400 rather than counting the halvings.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the plum pudding model of the atom was replaced by the nuclear model. Refer to the experimental evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states an experiment was done with gold foil.
Secure: the Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil; most passed straight through (consistent with mostly empty space), but some were deflected and a few bounced straight back — this was not predicted by the plum pudding model (which assumed a diffuse positive charge and would allow all particles through with only small deflections).
Mastering: as Secure, plus explains that bouncing back required a tiny, very dense, positively charged region (nucleus) repelling the positive alpha particles — the nuclear model was proposed to fit this evidence; the model was accepted because it explained all the observations.

[1 mark: experiment correctly described (alpha particles, gold foil); 1 mark: key result described (most pass through, some deflect, few bounce back); 1 mark: explains why the plum pudding model could not account for the results and what the nuclear model proposed]

practice_questions.text:
Balance the following nuclear equation for the alpha decay of polonium-210:
\(^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z}\text{Pb} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}\)
State the values of A and Z.
practice_questions.marks:
A = 210 − 4 = 206 [1 mark]
Z = 84 − 2 = 82 [1 mark]

So the daughter nucleus is \(^{206}_{82}\text{Pb}\) (lead-206).

Verification: 210 = 206 + 4 ✓; 84 = 82 + 2 ✓.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between contamination by a radioactive material and irradiation by a radioactive source. In your answer, discuss how the half-life of a material affects the hazard it presents.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: distinguishes contamination (source inside body) from irradiation (external source).
Secure:
- Contamination: radioactive material deposited on or inside the body; source continues to irradiate nearby tissue even if the external source is moved away — ongoing risk.
- Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; risk ceases when the source is removed.
