- Half-life significance: a long half-life means slow decay, so the material remains hazardous for a long time; a very short half-life decays quickly but initially high activity poses an acute risk; in contamination, short half-life may be preferable in medical contexts (e.g. tracers) as activity decreases quickly inside the body.
Mastering: as Secure, plus discusses which radiation type is most dangerous in each context (alpha is strongly ionising inside the body — dangerous in contamination; less hazardous as irradiation because it is stopped by skin); links this to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis when making decisions about using radioactive materials in medicine.

[1 mark: contamination correctly defined; 1 mark: irradiation correctly defined and contrasted; 1 mark: explains why contamination is more hazardous; 1 mark: half-life linked to duration of hazard; 1 mark: named radiation type linked to contamination vs irradiation hazard]

practice_questions.text: A patient is given a radioactive tracer for a medical scan. The tracer has a half-life of 6 hours and an initial activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the activity after 24 hours, and explain why a short half-life is preferred for medical tracers.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculation [3 marks]:
24 hours = 4 half-lives (24 ÷ 6 = 4) [1 mark]
Fraction remaining = \((\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{1}{16}\) [1 mark]
Activity = \(800 \times \frac{1}{16} = 50\) Bq [1 mark]

Explanation [3 marks]:
Emerging: states a short half-life is safer.
Secure: short half-life means the tracer decays rapidly, so the patient is only exposed to significant radiation for a short time; the activity falls to safe levels quickly, reducing the total radiation dose to the patient.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes the trade-off — the half-life must be long enough for imaging to be completed before the activity falls too low (risk-benefit: IaS4); also acknowledges that gamma-emitting tracers are used because gamma rays pass out of the body for detection, while alpha emitters inside the body would cause greater cell damage due to high ionising power.

[1 mark: correct calculation of 4 half-lives; 1 mark: activity = 50 Bq; 1 mark: correct fraction remaining used; 1 mark: short half-life reduces radiation dose after scan; 1 mark: must be long enough to complete the scan — trade-off identified; 1 mark: gamma emitter preferred / alpha would be most dangerous internally]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the variation must be heritable for natural selection to produce evolutionary change.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Heritable variation is encoded in DNA and passed from parents to offspring.
1 mark: Only heritable variation can accumulate across generations; non-heritable environmental variation disappears when the individual dies and does not affect the population's characteristics.

practice_questions.text: Describe how natural selection could lead to a population of rabbits becoming better camouflaged in a habitat where a new predator has arrived.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random variation in fur colour exists in the population [1]; the new predator is a selection pressure, killing rabbits with less effective camouflage more often [1]; rabbits with better camouflage survive and reproduce, passing on the variant to offspring; over many generations, better camouflage becomes more common [1].
Secure: Variation exists [1]; predator selects for camouflage [1]; camouflage becomes more common over generations.
Developing: States camouflaged rabbits survive without describing the mechanism.
Emerging: States rabbits change colour.

practice_questions.text: Compare the fossil record and DNA evidence as two sources of evidence for evolution, explaining what each tells us and one limitation of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fossil record shows changes in organisms over geological time and confirms simple organisms precede complex ones [1]; limitation: the fossil record is incomplete, not all organisms fossilise [1]. DNA evidence shows more similar DNA in more closely related species [1]; limitation: requires intact DNA, which degrades; ancient specimens hard to sequence [1].
Secure: One strength and one limitation of each.
Developing: Describes one source only.
Emerging: Names the fossil record without evaluating it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of geographic isolation in the process of speciation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Geographic isolation prevents interbreeding between the two sub-populations [1]; each population then experiences different selection pressures and different mutations accumulate [1]; over many generations genetic differences accumulate until reproductive isolation is complete — the two groups can no longer produce fertile offspring even if reunited [1].
Secure: Isolation prevents interbreeding [1]; different selection pressures lead to divergence [1].
Developing: States the populations become separate.
Emerging: Mentions isolation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how understanding natural selection can help scientists predict and respond to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Resistance arises through mutation [1]; antibiotic use selects for resistant variants by killing susceptible bacteria [1]; resistant strains reproduce and spread [1]; prediction: overuse and misuse will accelerate resistance [1]; response: prescribe only when necessary, complete courses, develop new antibiotics, monitor resistant strains [1].
Secure: Three valid points with clear reasoning.
Developing: States resistance spreads; one response suggested.
Emerging: States bacteria become resistant.

practice_questions.text: State the years in which Darwin and Wallace jointly presented their ideas and the year Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Joint presentation 1858; publication of On the Origin of Species 1859. Both dates are needed for the mark.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the function of a relay neurone?
A) It carries impulses from a receptor to the CNS
B) It connects sensory neurones to motor neurones within the CNS
C) It carries impulses from the CNS to a muscle or gland
D) It releases neurotransmitters into the bloodstream
practice_questions.marks: B) It connects sensory neurones to motor neurones within the CNS [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a reflex action and give one example.
practice_questions.marks: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought [1 mark]; example: withdrawing from pain / blinking / pupil constriction in bright light [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a signal crosses a synapse. Include the role of neurotransmitters in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An electrical impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone [1 mark]; neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap [1 mark]; they diffuse across and bind to receptor proteins on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three steps.
Developing: Mentions neurotransmitters crossing the gap but lacks the receptor-binding step.
Emerging: Vague reference to chemicals carrying signals.

practice_questions.text: A student touches a hot pan and immediately withdraws their hand before feeling pain. Using the reflex arc, explain why their hand moved before they felt pain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The reflex arc uses a relay neurone in the spinal cord [1 mark]; the motor signal to the hand muscles is sent from the spinal cord directly (without waiting for the brain to process the signal) [1 mark]; the hand withdraws before the sensory signal has time to travel all the way to the brain and produce a conscious experience of pain [1 mark]; a separate signal does travel to the brain after the reflex, which is when pain is felt [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four points.
Developing: States the reflex bypasses the brain but without mechanistic detail.
Emerging: Correctly states the hand moves before feeling pain without scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the structure of a myelinated axon is adapted to transmit impulses more rapidly.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer around the axon [1 mark]; it prevents electrical signals from leaking across the axon membrane [1 mark]; this means the impulse travels much faster along the axon than in a neurone with no myelin sheath [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points.
Developing: States myelin insulates the axon but does not explain how this speeds transmission.
Emerging: Identifies myelin as an insulator.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of reflex actions to human survival. Consider both the advantages and any situations where reflexes could be disadvantageous.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Advantages: Reflexes are much faster than voluntary responses so they protect the body from harm before damage occurs [1 mark]; they are automatic, so no mental energy is required — voluntary attention is freed for other tasks [1 mark]; examples: withdrawing from pain, pupil reflex preventing retinal damage [1 mark].
Disadvantages / limitations: Reflexes cannot be adapted to context — a reflex response may occur even when it is not the best action [1 mark]; in some situations the brain can modify a reflex response, for example to stop us dropping a hot object [1 mark].
Conclusion: Overall, reflexes are highly beneficial for survival by providing instant protection, outweighing occasional cases where an automatic response is unhelpful [1 mark].
Secure: Both advantages and limitations addressed, conclusion present.
Developing: Advantages only, limited analysis.
Emerging: States reflexes are fast and helpful without further development.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'dynamic equilibrium' in a reversible reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction (1); concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, but the reaction has not stopped — both directions are still occurring (1). Secure: both points. Developing: one point only. Emerging: 'forward and reverse reactions happen' without specifying rate equality.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process uses a temperature of approximately 450°C. The forward reaction making ammonia is exothermic. Explain why a lower temperature would give a higher yield but is not used industrially.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: lower temperature favours the exothermic direction by Le Chatelier's principle, increasing equilibrium yield of ammonia (1); however, lower temperature reduces the rate of reaction — it would take too long to produce a useful amount (1); 450°C is a compromise: it gives a reasonable yield with a rate fast enough to be economically viable (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: The equation for the Haber process is: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Explain why high pressure increases the yield of ammonia, and suggest why a pressure of approximately 200 atmospheres is chosen rather than a much higher pressure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: there are 4 moles of gas on the left (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and 2 on the right (2 NH₃) (1); high pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer moles of gas, i.e. towards the products, increasing yield (1); very high pressures require costly, reinforced equipment and are dangerous to operate (1); 200 atm is a compromise between acceptable yield and manageable cost and safety (1) — 4 marks max. Secure: 3 marks. Developing: 2 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process. In your answer, state what the catalyst does and does not affect.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the iron catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions (1); it allows equilibrium to be reached more quickly (1); it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield — it only reduces the time to reach equilibrium (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: 'it speeds up the reaction' without addressing equilibrium position.

practice_questions.text: In the Haber process, the yield of ammonia at the operating conditions is moderate. Explain how the industrial process overcomes this limitation to produce ammonia economically.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the ammonia is continuously removed from the reaction vessel by cooling and condensing it to a liquid (1); removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium to the right to replace it, producing more ammonia (Le Chatelier) (1); unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back into the reaction vessel (1); this means the raw materials are not wasted (1); over time, the overall yield of the process is much greater than the equilibrium yield suggests (1). Secure: 3–4 points. Developing: 2 points. Emerging: 1 point.

practice_questions.text: Ammonia produced by the Haber process is used to make nitrogen fertilisers. Explain one environmental problem that can arise from the use of nitrogen fertilisers on farmland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: nitrogen fertilisers can wash off fields into rivers or lakes in rain (1); this causes excessive algal growth (eutrophication) because algae use the extra nitrates as nutrients (1); the algae block light, and when they die, decomposing bacteria deplete oxygen in the water, harming or killing aquatic life (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: 'causes pollution' without explaining mechanism.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'potable water'?
A) Water that contains no dissolved substances
B) Water that has been boiled
C) Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms
D) Water that has only been filtered through sand
practice_questions.marks: C) Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two methods that can be used to sterilise water during the treatment of fresh water.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two from: chlorine (or chlorine compounds) (1); ozone (1); ultraviolet light (UV) (1). Award 1 mark per correct method, max 2.
Secure: Two methods named correctly.
Developing: One method named.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe how fresh water is treated to make it potable. Include the key stages in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Filtration — passes water through gravel/sand filter beds to remove large particles (1); sedimentation — fine particles settle out in settlement tanks (1); sterilisation — chlorine/ozone/UV used to kill microorganisms (1).
Secure: All three stages named with brief explanation.
Developing: Two stages named correctly.
Emerging: One stage named.

practice_questions.text: Compare distillation and reverse osmosis as methods of desalination. Include in your answer one advantage and one disadvantage shared by both methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both produce potable water from sea water (1); both require large amounts of energy, making them expensive (1); distillation works by boiling sea water and condensing the steam (1); reverse osmosis forces water under pressure through a semi-permeable membrane (1).
Secure: Both methods correctly described with shared disadvantage.
Developing: One method described accurately.
Emerging: Names one method only.

practice_questions.text: A student is investigating three water samples — tap water, sea water and distilled water — by testing for the presence of chloride ions using silver nitrate solution. Plan the investigation, identifying the key variables and one safety precaution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Independent variable: which water sample is tested (1); dependent variable: whether a precipitate forms / the result of the silver nitrate test (1); control variables: volume of each sample used / concentration of silver nitrate / temperature (1); safety: silver nitrate stains skin and clothing and is an irritant — wear eye protection and gloves (1).
Secure: Variables correct plus safety.
Developing: Variables identified but safety missing or vice versa.
Emerging: General description without variable identification.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of desalination as a solution to water scarcity, considering both its advantages and its limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantages: desalination can produce potable water from sea water, making it valuable in regions with limited fresh water sources (1); it is not dependent on rainfall or river flow (1). Limitations: both distillation and reverse osmosis require large amounts of energy (1); this makes desalination expensive (1); if powered by fossil fuels, desalination itself contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, potentially worsening the climate change that is reducing water availability in some regions (1). Overall evaluation: desalination is an important technology in water-scarce regions but is not a universal solution — renewable energy-powered desalination would address the carbon cost but remains expensive at scale (1).
Secure: Four points with a weighing statement.
Developing: Lists advantages and limitations without weighing.
Emerging: One-sided response.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following equations is correctly balanced?
A) H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
B) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
C) H₂ + O → H₂O
D) H₂ + 2O → 2H₂O
practice_questions.marks: B) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.
(Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
Describe the steps a student should follow to balance the symbol equation for the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid: Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
practice_questions.marks: Count Mg: 1=1, balanced [1]; count Cl: right has 2, so put 2 in front of HCl [1]; check H: left has 2 (from 2HCl), right has 2 (H₂) — balanced. Final equation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ [1].

practice_questions.text:
Calculate the mass of water produced when 80 g of methane (CH₄) undergoes complete combustion.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
(Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
Show all your working.
practice_questions.marks: Mr of CH₄ = 12 + 4(1) = 16 g/mol [1]; moles of CH₄ = 80 ÷ 16 = 5 mol [1]; ratio 1:2 so moles of H₂O = 10 mol [1]; mass of H₂O = 10 × 18 = 180 g [1].

practice_questions.text: A scientist finds that when 2.4 g of magnesium burns in air, a white solid with a mass greater than 2.4 g is produced. A student claims this contradicts the law of conservation of mass. Evaluate whether the student is correct, using your knowledge of conservation of mass and what happens during combustion.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the student is incorrect [1]; conservation of mass applies to all atoms involved in the reaction, including from the air [1]; magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide [1]; the mass of oxygen from the air is added to the magnesium [1]; total mass of reactants (Mg + O₂) equals total mass of product (MgO) [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: identifies product is heavier and involves oxygen but does not fully apply conservation.

practice_questions.text:
Zinc oxide reacts with carbon to produce zinc and carbon dioxide:
2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO₂
(Ar: Zn = 65, O = 16, C = 12)
Calculate the mass of zinc produced from 18.1 g of zinc oxide, and explain what the molar ratio in the equation tells you about the reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Mr ZnO = 65 + 16 = 81 g/mol [1]; moles ZnO = 18.1 ÷ 81 = 0.223 mol [1]; ratio 2:2 so moles Zn = 0.223 mol [1]; mass Zn = 0.223 × 65 = 14.5 g [1]; explanation: coefficients show the relative number of moles of each substance reacting [1]; 2 mol ZnO reacts with 1 mol C to give 2 mol Zn and 1 mol CO₂ — this fixed ratio cannot be changed [1]. Secure: four calculation marks. Developing: correct Mr and moles only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what red-shift is, and describe how observations of red-shift from distant galaxies support the Big Bang model.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Red-shift is the increase in observed wavelength (shift towards the red end of the spectrum) of light from a galaxy moving away from us (1). More distant galaxies show greater red-shift, meaning they are receding faster (1). This pattern applies in all directions (1). Running the expansion backward in time suggests the universe was once much smaller, hotter and denser (1). This is consistent with the Big Bang model — the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since (1). The cosmic microwave background provides independent supporting evidence — a faint microwave glow from all directions, interpreted as cooled remnant radiation from the early universe (1). Secure: Four or five valid points with a clear logical link. Developing: Describes red-shift and expanding universe but does not link them explicitly to Big Bang. Emerging: Names red-shift without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of events in the formation of a star from a cloud of gas and dust, up to the point at which it becomes a stable main sequence star.
practice_questions.marks: Gravity pulls gas cloud together (1). As gas is compressed, its temperature rises (work is done on it by compression) (1). When core temperature is high enough, nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins; outward radiation pressure balances gravitational collapse and the star becomes stable (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why an object moving in a circular orbit has a constantly changing velocity even if its speed does not change.
practice_questions.marks: Velocity is a vector — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction (1). In circular orbit the direction of motion changes continuously, so velocity changes even though speed (the magnitude) remains constant (1).

practice_questions.text: The light from a distant galaxy shows that a particular spectral line has a wavelength of 520 nm. The same line measured in the laboratory has a wavelength of 500 nm. State whether this galaxy is moving towards or away from Earth, and justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Moving away from Earth (1). The observed wavelength (520 nm) is longer than the laboratory value (500 nm) — this is red-shift, indicating the galaxy is receding (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how increasing improvements in telescope technology over the last 100 years have affected scientific confidence in the Big Bang model, using the concept of scientific models and evidence.
practice_questions.marks: Improved telescopes allow detection of fainter, more distant galaxies (1). Observations at wavelengths beyond visible light (e.g. microwave for CMB, infrared, X-ray) are possible from space without atmospheric interference (1). Each new dataset either supports or challenges the Big Bang model; repeated independent confirmation increases confidence (IaS3) (1). For example, refined measurements of the CMB by satellite missions have confirmed its temperature and uniformity to high precision, matching Big Bang predictions (1). No major observations have overturned the model; instead they have added detail (e.g. dark energy driving accelerated expansion) — illustrating that scientific models evolve but are not abandoned lightly when evidence is inconsistent (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the eventual fate of a star similar in mass to the Sun with the eventual fate of a star much more massive than the Sun.
practice_questions.marks: Sun-like star: expands into a red giant as hydrogen runs low (1); sheds outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a cooling white dwarf (1). Massive star: also expands (red supergiant), but core collapses catastrophically once iron accumulates (1); outer layers explode as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why preclinical testing cannot guarantee that a drug will be safe in humans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Human physiology differs from animal physiology [1]; effects observed in animal models or cell cultures may not replicate in the human body [1].
Secure: States that animals and humans are different, so results may not apply to humans.
Developing: Says animals are not humans.
Emerging: Says testing is done on animals.

practice_questions.text: A new antibiotic is tested in a clinical trial. Half the patients receive the antibiotic; half receive a placebo. Neither the patients nor the doctors administering treatment know who is in which group. Explain what type of trial this is and why this design is important.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies double-blind trial [1]; explains that neither patient nor researcher knows who is in which group, preventing bias in symptom reporting and administration [1]; placebo controls for the placebo effect so any improvement in the antibiotic group can be attributed to the drug [1].
Secure: Names double-blind [1]; explains one source of bias it removes [1].
Developing: States neither group knows, without explaining why this matters.
Emerging: Describes the design without linking it to reliability.

practice_questions.text: Describe how antibiotic resistance develops in a bacterial population over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random mutation gives some bacteria a survival advantage against the antibiotic [1]; these bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring [1]; over time the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population [1].
Secure: Mutation leads to resistance [1]; resistant bacteria reproduce more [1].
Developing: States bacteria become resistant after exposure, without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Says bacteria get used to the antibiotic.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that results from a clinical trial funded by the company manufacturing the drug provide reliable evidence for its effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States trials can still be rigorous regardless of funding [1]; identifies conflict of interest as a genuine concern (company may benefit financially from positive results) [1]; reporting bias — positive results more likely to be published than negative ones [1]; peer review provides some protection [1]; independent replication by separate groups strengthens confidence [1]; balanced conclusion weighing evidence quality against potential bias [1].
Secure: Identifies conflict of interest [1]; one further valid evaluative point [1]; limited conclusion.
Developing: States company funding may be biased without explaining mechanism.
Emerging: Simply agrees or disagrees without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why antibiotics are not prescribed for viral infections such as influenza.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by targeting bacterial structures; they have no effect on viruses (accept: viruses lack the structures that antibiotics target).

practice_questions.text: A clinical trial for a new pain-relief drug has 40 participants in total. Suggest two ways in which the reliability of the trial could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid improvements: Increase the sample size (40 is very small) [1]; use a double-blind design if not already in place [1]; ensure randomisation of participants to drug/placebo groups [1]; extend the trial duration to detect long-term effects or delayed side effects [1]. (Accept any two.)

practice_questions.text: State the equation for calculating mean rate of reaction when measuring gas volume.
practice_questions.marks: Award: mean rate = volume of gas produced (cm³) ÷ time (s). Accept equivalent with correct units.

practice_questions.text: A student dissolves 3.6 g of sodium chloride in 200 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration of the solution in g/dm³.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: converts 200 cm³ to 0.2 dm³ (1), concentration = 3.6 ÷ 0.2 = 18 g/dm³ (1).
Secure: method correct, conversion error only.
Developing: correct equation but volume not converted.
Emerging: equation stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid produces 60 cm³ of gas in 30 s, then the reaction stops. Calculate the mean rate over the entire reaction and explain why the rate decreased as the reaction continued.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mean rate = 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s (1); rate decreased because zinc (or acid) was used up, so there are fewer reactant particles and collision frequency decreases (2).
Secure: mean rate correct, explanation partial (mentions ‘less reactant’ without linking to collisions).
Developing: mean rate correct, no explanation.
Emerging: calculation attempted but significant error.

practice_questions.text: A rate-of-reaction graph shows the volume of gas produced over time for two experiments: one with acid concentration 1 mol/dm³ and one with 2 mol/dm³. Compare the gradients of the two curves at the start and suggest what you would see in the final volumes of gas collected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: higher concentration has steeper initial gradient = faster rate at start (1); collision frequency increases at higher concentration (1); both experiments produce the same final volume of gas (1) because the amount of zinc (the solid) is the limiting reactant (1).
Secure: gradients compared correctly, final volume reasoning present.
Developing: gradients correct, final volume not explained.
Emerging: states one curve is steeper without explanation.

practice_questions.text: 0.4 mol of potassium hydroxide is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³ (1); concentration = 0.4 ÷ 0.25 = 1.6 mol/dm³ (1).
Secure: correct method, arithmetic error accepted.
Developing: correct division but dm³ conversion missing.
Emerging: equation recalled but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A chemist investigates how a catalyst affects the rate of a reaction. The uncatalysed reaction takes 120 s to produce 30 cm³ of gas; the catalysed reaction produces the same volume in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate for each reaction, compare the rates and explain, using collision theory and the concept of activation energy, why the catalyst increases the rate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: uncatalysed rate = 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25 cm³/s (1); catalysed rate = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 cm³/s (1); catalyst increases rate threefold (1); catalyst provides alternative pathway with lower activation energy (1); more collisions now have sufficient energy to react (1); catalyst is unchanged at end of reaction (1).
Secure: both rates correct, activation energy reasoning present, one element missing.
Developing: one rate correct, catalyst effect described.
Emerging: rates attempted, activation energy not mentioned.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the main steps in the process of genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: four steps described in sequence — isolating the required gene; inserting it into a vector (e.g. plasmid); using the vector to deliver the gene into host cells; selecting cells that have incorporated and expressed the gene. Each step clearly linked to the next. Secure: three steps correctly described in order; one step missing or vague. Developing: two steps correctly described; sequence not always logical. Emerging: general statement about changing DNA without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: State two uses of genetic testing in healthcare.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any two of — identifying carriers of recessive alleles for family planning; identifying alleles that cause or increase risk of specific conditions; enabling personalised medicine (matching drug to genetic profile). One mark each. Secure: two uses stated but one lacks precision. Developing: one correct use. Emerging: vague reference to 'finding out about diseases' without precision.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain the role of a plasmid as a vector in genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: plasmid is a small circular DNA molecule found in bacteria; it acts as a vector by carrying the desired gene; it is introduced into bacterial host cells, which then incorporate and express the gene to produce the desired protein. Secure: plasmid's carrier role described and linked to bacterial cells; one point missing or vague. Developing: states plasmid carries a gene but does not explain delivery to cells or protein production. Emerging: mentions plasmid without explaining its function.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of genetic modification to produce human insulin for treating diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies benefit (reliable, large-scale supply of human insulin; reduced immune reactions compared to animal-sourced insulin); identifies risk (potential for GM bacteria to spread outside controlled environment; ethical concerns about engineering organisms); weighs benefits against risks (benefits clearly significant for millions of patients; risks are managed by containment in fermenters; conclusion that benefits outweigh risks in this case); notes regulatory oversight. Secure: benefits and risks both present; weighing attempted but not fully developed; conclusion present. Developing: benefits and risks listed but not weighed against each other; no conclusion. Emerging: only one side (benefits or risks) addressed.

practice_questions.text: A couple are found to be carriers of a recessive genetic condition. Discuss the benefits and risks of genetic testing in this context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies benefit of testing (informed family planning decisions; possible IVF with embryo selection); notes prenatal testing risk (small risk of miscarriage if amniocentesis used; false positives/negatives); discusses the couple's right to make their own decisions balanced against the benefit to potential future children; addresses the psychological impact of knowing vs not knowing; reaches a balanced conclusion. Secure: benefits and risks both addressed with reference to the specific scenario; weighing attempted. Developing: benefits and risks noted but not applied to the couple's scenario specifically. Emerging: general statements about genetic testing without engaging with the couple's context.

practice_questions.text: Describe one potential risk of releasing genetically modified mosquitoes into the environment.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any one valid risk stated clearly — e.g. long-term ecological effects on predators that feed on mosquitoes are unpredictable; potential for the gene to spread beyond the target species; reduction in mosquito population could disrupt food chains. One mark for one precise risk.

before.exam_tip_html: Evaluate questions on gene technology are common extended-response questions. The mark scheme rewards answers that present both benefits AND risks, and that then weigh them against each other to reach a conclusion. Simply listing risks or benefits without comparison will cap your score at the lower bands. Use specific named examples (insulin production, named crop or mosquito programme) rather than vague statements. When asked about genetic testing specifically, include the distinction between tests that detect certain disease (single-gene disorders) and those that assess probabilistic risk (complex conditions).

practice_questions.text: State the voltage and frequency of the UK mains electricity supply, and identify whether it is alternating or direct current.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: approximately 230 V, alternating current (a.c.)
1 mark: frequency of 50 Hz

Emerging: states voltage only or describes as a.c. without frequency.
Developing: states voltage and a.c. but omits frequency, or gives frequency without voltage.
Secure: correctly states ~230 V, a.c., 50 Hz.

practice_questions.text: A laptop charger is rated at 45 W and plugged into the 230 V mains. Calculate the current drawn by the charger.
practice_questions.marks:
\(I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{45}{230} = 0.196\) A (accept 0.20 A)

1 mark for correct rearrangement and substitution.
1 mark for correct answer with unit (A).

Common error: dividing V by P instead of P by V.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the live wire in a mains plug is dangerous even when the appliance is switched off.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states the live wire is at high voltage.
Secure: explains the live wire is at mains voltage (approximately 230 V) relative to earth, even with the switch open, because the switch breaks the circuit on the appliance side not the supply side.
Mastering: extends to explain that touching the live wire creates a potential difference between the person and earth, driving a current through the body, which can cause serious injury.

[1 mark: live wire remains at mains voltage/potential difference relative to earth; 1 mark: switch is on the appliance side so does not disconnect the live wire from supply; 1 mark: touching live wire causes current to flow through the body to earth]

practice_questions.text:
A 2.5 kW electric heater is used for 90 minutes.
(a) Calculate the energy transferred in joules.
(b) Calculate the charge that flows if the heater operates at 230 V.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Convert: 2.5 kW = 2500 W; 90 min = 5400 s
\(E = Pt = 2500 \times 5400 = 13{,}500{,}000\) J (13.5 MJ) [2 marks: 1 for correct conversion, 1 for final answer with unit]

(b) \(Q = \frac{E}{V} = \frac{13{,}500{,}000}{230} \approx 58{,}696\) C (accept 58,700 C) [2 marks: 1 for correct equation/substitution, 1 for answer with unit C]

Common error: failing to convert kW to W or minutes to seconds.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the equation for power loss in cables (\(P = I^2 R\)), why the National Grid transmits electrical energy at high voltage rather than low voltage.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states that high voltage means low current.
Secure: uses \(P = IV\) to explain that for the same power, increasing voltage requires a smaller current, and then applies \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\) to show that less current means less power lost as heat.
Mastering: fully chains the argument — power transmitted is constant; step-up transformer increases voltage, so current decreases proportionally; since power loss \(= I^2 R\), squaring the smaller current gives a much smaller loss, making high-voltage transmission significantly more efficient.

[1 mark: high voltage → lower current for same power; 1 mark: power loss = I²R, so lower current means less heat loss in cables; 1 mark: links to transformer action stepping up voltage at the generating station]

practice_questions.text:
A student tests three appliances and records their power ratings: a lamp (100 W), a kettle (2200 W) and a phone charger (10 W). All operate at 230 V.
Select the correct fuse rating (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) for the kettle and justify your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: selects 13 A fuse without calculation.
Developing: calculates current \(I = P/V = 2200/230 \approx 9.6\) A and selects 13 A, but explanation is limited.
Secure: calculates \(I \approx 9.6\) A; explains the fuse must be rated just above the normal operating current, so 13 A is chosen (a 5 A fuse would blow under normal use; a 13 A fuse protects against dangerous currents above ~13 A).
Mastering: as Secure, plus explains the fuse is in the live wire so it breaks the circuit before the cable can overheat; notes that using too high a rating defeats the purpose of the safety device; may contrast with the lamp (\(I \approx 0.43\) A → 3 A fuse) to show selection depends on appliance power.

[6 marks total: 2 for correct calculation and fuse selection; 2 for clear explanation of selection logic; 2 for explaining fuse purpose in context of safety]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of insulin?
A) It raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to convert glycogen to glucose
B) It lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen
C) It is released by the pituitary gland in response to low blood glucose
D) It prevents ovulation by inhibiting FSH and LH
practice_questions.marks: B) It lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: Type 1: the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, so no insulin is produced [1 mark]; type 2: body cells become less sensitive/resistant to insulin, so it has less effect [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the role of ADH in regulating water balance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: When blood water potential falls, the pituitary gland releases ADH [1 mark]; ADH travels to the kidneys and makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water [1 mark]; more water is reabsorbed into the blood, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine, restoring water potential by negative feedback [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three steps.
Developing: States ADH causes kidneys to reabsorb water but lacks the trigger and feedback.
Emerging: Names ADH without explaining its mechanism.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how the four hormones of the menstrual cycle interact to produce ovulation around day 14.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: FSH from the pituitary gland causes follicle maturation in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen production [1 mark]; oestrogen causes the uterus lining to thicken and, at high levels, triggers a surge of LH [1 mark]; the LH surge triggers ovulation (release of the egg) at around day 14 [1 mark]; progesterone is then produced by the empty follicle to maintain the lining; if no fertilisation occurs, progesterone falls and menstruation begins [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the four mechanisms.
Developing: Names the hormones without linking them in sequence.
Emerging: States ovulation occurs at day 14 without hormonal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A patient with type 1 diabetes tests their blood glucose before breakfast and finds it is well above the normal range, despite not having eaten. Explain why blood glucose can be high in type 1 diabetes even without eating, and describe how the patient could lower it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In type 1 diabetes, no insulin is produced [1 mark]; overnight, the liver still converts glycogen to glucose and releases it into the blood (normal background glucose release) [1 mark]; without insulin, cells cannot take up this glucose and the liver cannot store it as glycogen [1 mark]; blood glucose therefore rises; the patient would inject insulin to stimulate glucose uptake by cells [1 mark]; they should also monitor carbohydrate intake and exercise levels, as both affect blood glucose [1 mark].
Secure: Four of the five points.
Developing: States no insulin is made and injection is needed, without mechanistic explanation.
Emerging: Identifies type 1 as lacking insulin.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of hormonal contraception to control fertility. In your answer, consider how it works, its effectiveness and any ethical considerations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
Mechanism: maintains high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, inhibiting FSH and LH release, preventing ovulation [up to 2 marks].
Benefits: highly effective when used correctly; some forms are long-acting (implant, injection) and do not require daily action; can also reduce symptoms of conditions like endometriosis [1 mark].
Limitations/risks: does not protect against sexually transmitted infections; some individuals experience side effects (mood changes, nausea, blood clot risk for some types); ethical objection from some religious or personal viewpoints about using hormones to prevent natural fertility [up to 2 marks].
Conclusion: Weighs effectiveness against risks and ethical concerns [1 mark].
Secure: Mechanism plus benefits and one concern.
Developing: Mechanism described only.
Emerging: Vague reference to the pill preventing pregnancy.

practice_questions.text: A block of material has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
Describe what happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state, and explain why.
practice_questions.marks: The temperature does not change during a change of state [1 mark]. The energy supplied is used to break the forces between particles (changing their arrangement), not to increase their kinetic energy [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States temperature stays constant but gives no explanation in terms of particles.

practice_questions.text: A 3 kg copper block is cooled from 200 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J/kg/°C. Calculate the energy released by the block.
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly identifies the temperature change and substitutes into the equation but makes an arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: A kettle contains 1.5 kg of water at 20 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4,200 J/kg/°C. Calculate the energy needed to bring the water to 100 °C. Then calculate the additional energy needed to boil the water away completely. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2,260,000 J/kg.
practice_questions.marks: Energy to heat: ΔE = 1.5 × 4200 × (100 − 20) = 1.5 × 4200 × 80 = 504,000 J [1 mark]. Energy to vaporise: E = m × L = 1.5 × 2,260,000 = 3,390,000 J [1 mark]. Total energy = 504,000 + 3,390,000 = 3,894,000 J [1 mark]. The vaporisation energy is much larger than the heating energy [1 mark — accept comparison that latent heat of vaporisation >> heat energy for same mass].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Both energies calculated correctly, comparison made.
Developing: Heating energy correct but error in latent heat calculation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an object with an average density less than water will float, using the equation for density in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Density = mass ÷ volume [1 mark]. If an object's average density is less than 1,000 kg/m³ (the density of water), it displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight before it is fully submerged [1 mark], so the upward force of the water (upthrust) balances its weight and it floats [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that lower density objects float but does not connect to density equation or displaced water.

practice_questions.text: A student heats equal masses of water and vegetable oil using identical heaters. The oil heats up faster. Evaluate what this tells us about the specific heat capacities of the two substances, and explain one practical application of this difference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses ΔE = mcΔΘ — for the same ΔE (same heater, same time) and same m, a larger ΔΘ means smaller c. Therefore vegetable oil has a lower SHC than water. Quantifies the reasoning: if oil heats twice as fast, its SHC is half that of water. Explains a practical application: water's high SHC makes it ideal as a coolant in car engines (absorbs large amounts of thermal energy per kg without large temperature rise) or in central heating systems (transports large amounts of thermal energy). Alternatively: cooking in oil is faster because oil's lower SHC allows it to reach higher temperatures more quickly with less energy input.
Secure: Correctly deduces oil has lower SHC using the equation; gives one valid application.
Developing: Correctly deduces oil has lower SHC but without reference to the equation; application unclear.
Emerging: States oil heats faster without connecting to SHC.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'nanoparticle'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Particles with dimensions in the range 1–100 nm (1 mark); with the implication that properties differ from the bulk form of the same material (1 mark). Secure: correct size range given. Developing: 'very small particles' without the nm range. Emerging: no size reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why nanoparticles of a substance may behave differently from a large piece of the same substance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio (1); a greater proportion of atoms are on the surface and available for interactions (1); this changes properties such as reactivity, conductivity, or colour (1). Secure: surface area to volume ratio mentioned and linked to changed properties. Developing: surface area mentioned without ratio or consequence. Emerging: 'they are smaller' only.

practice_questions.text: A scientist is investigating the use of silver nanoparticles in food packaging. Evaluate the use of silver nanoparticles in this application, considering both the evidence for benefits and the risks involved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefit — antimicrobial properties inhibit bacterial growth, extending shelf life and reducing food waste (2); risk — nanoparticles can cross cell membranes and may be toxic; evidence on long-term effects in humans is not yet conclusive (2); balanced judgement — current evidence may support use in packaging where direct ingestion is minimal, pending further research (2). Secure: two benefits and two risks identified with some weighing. Developing: benefits and risks listed but not weighed. Emerging: only one side discussed.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer produces reusable stainless steel water bottles. Outline the four stages you would examine in a life cycle assessment (LCA) of this product.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for correctly identifying and briefly explaining: (1) extraction and processing of raw materials (steel from iron ore); (2) manufacture, packaging and transport; (3) use of the product; (4) end-of-life disposal, recycling, or reuse. Mastering: all four with specific examples relevant to steel. Secure: all four stages named. Developing: three stages. Emerging: one or two stages.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'If a product can be recycled, its LCA will always show a lower environmental impact than a non-recyclable product.' Evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: recycling does reduce resource extraction and often energy use at end of life (1); however, LCAs depend on assumptions — recycling rates vary in practice, collection and sorting have energy costs (1); manufacturing stage may dominate impact regardless of end-of-life route (1); LCA conclusions depend on weighting of different impact categories, introducing subjectivity (1); therefore the claim is an oversimplification — the full picture requires examining all four stages (1). Secure: 3–4 points with some nuance. Developing: 2 points, limited analysis. Emerging: simple agree/disagree without evidence.

practice_questions.text: A food manufacturer compares the environmental impact of glass jars and plastic tubs for packaging jam. Suggest two limitations of using a life cycle assessment to make this comparison.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations: LCAs involve assumptions about end-of-life disposal which may not reflect actual consumer behaviour; comparing different types of environmental impact (e.g. water use vs carbon emissions) requires value judgements; results can be influenced by who commissions the LCA; data on all stages may not be fully available. Mastering: two distinct, well-explained limitations. Secure: two limitations briefly stated. Developing: one limitation. Emerging: vague answer.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines biodiversity?
A) The number of individual organisms in a habitat
B) The variety of life in an area — its organisms, their genes and its ecosystems
C) The total mass of all organisms in an ecosystem
D) The rate at which new species evolve
practice_questions.marks: B) The variety of life in an area — its organisms, their genes and its ecosystems [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the binomial system of classification.
practice_questions.marks: A two-part naming system [1 mark] in which each species is given a unique Latin name consisting of its genus (capital) and species (lowercase) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how deforestation reduces biodiversity. In your answer, explain the mechanism by which habitat loss leads to species decline.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Deforestation removes the habitat (food, shelter, nesting sites) that species depend on [1 mark]; species that cannot survive elsewhere lose their population [1 mark]; knock-on effects through the food web cause further species decline as interdependencies break down [1 mark].
Secure: Two of the three points above, clearly linked.
Developing: One relevant point.
Emerging: Vague reference to animals being harmed.

practice_questions.text:
A scientist studying a meadow records 12 species of flowering plant, 8 species of insect and 3 species of bird. A nearby intensively farmed field has 2 plant species, 1 insect species and 1 bird species.
Explain why the meadow is more resilient to change than the farmed field, using the data above.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The meadow has far greater species richness (12 plant, 8 insect, 3 bird vs 2, 1, 1) [1 mark]; a more diverse food web means if one species declines, others can fill its role [1 mark]; pollinators in the meadow support plant reproduction, whereas the single insect species in the field is a critical dependency [1 mark]; loss of any one species in the farmed field is more likely to cascade and cause collapse [1 mark].
Secure: Three of the above points, using data appropriately.
Developing: One or two general points about biodiversity without data reference.
Emerging: States meadow has more species without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how captive breeding programmes and seed banks each contribute to maintaining biodiversity. Refer to the limitations of each approach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Captive breeding maintains populations of endangered animals so they do not become extinct [1 mark]; animals can be reintroduced to the wild once threats are managed [1 mark]; limitation: small captive population may have low genetic diversity (inbreeding) [1 mark]; seed banks preserve plant genetic diversity and can be used to reintroduce species [1 mark]; limitation: seeds may lose viability over time and the plants cannot be reintroduced if habitat is destroyed [1 mark].
Secure: Four of the above, with limitations addressed.
Developing: Benefits of one strategy described with limited attention to limitations.
Emerging: General statement that both help protect species.

practice_questions.text:
"Protecting biodiversity is more important than economic development."
Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider both the arguments for and against protecting biodiversity, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering:
For: Loss of species is irreversible; biodiversity supports ecosystem services (pollination, clean water, food); high-biodiversity ecosystems are more resilient to climate change; future species may have medical or scientific value not yet discovered [up to 3 marks for developed points].
Against: Economic development lifts communities out of poverty; sustainable land use can coexist with biodiversity; blanket protection may be seen as imposing costs on developing nations [up to 2 marks].
Conclusion: Justified conclusion that weighs the evidence — e.g. biodiversity loss is largely irreversible whereas economic damage can be recovered, suggesting biodiversity protection should have priority where trade-offs must be made [1 mark].
Secure: Both sides addressed, conclusion present but less developed.
Developing: One side only, limited development.
Emerging: Simple assertion without evidence.

before.exam_tip_html: For ‘Evaluate’ questions on conservation, always weigh both practical and ethical dimensions — examiners want to see reasoned judgement, not just a list of strategies. When writing the binomial name in an answer, remember: genus is capitalised, species is lowercase, and the whole name is italicised (underlined in handwriting). On ‘Explain why biodiversity matters’ questions, link biodiversity to ecosystem stability and to specific services humans rely on, such as pollination and food production — a vague “it’s good for nature” will not score full marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field at all times / retains its magnetism permanently.
1 mark: an induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed in an external field and loses its magnetism when the field is removed.

Note: induced magnets are always attracted to the source — never repelled.

practice_questions.text: A current-carrying wire of length 0.40 m is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. The current in the wire is 3.0 A. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice_questions.marks:
\(F = BIl = 0.25 \times 3.0 \times 0.40 = 0.30\) N

1 mark for correct substitution into \(F = BIl\).
1 mark for correct answer with unit (N).

Common error: using total wire length rather than only the length inside the field.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you could demonstrate that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field. State what equipment you would use and what you would observe.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states using a compass near a wire.
Secure: places a plotting compass near a straight wire carrying a current; observes that the compass needle deflects when current flows and returns to its original position when current is switched off; reversing the current reverses the needle deflection.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that the field lines form concentric circles around the wire, and increasing the current produces a greater deflection (stronger field).

[1 mark: compass near current-carrying wire; 1 mark: needle deflects when current flows / returns when current off; 1 mark: reversing current reverses deflection / field lines are concentric circles]

practice_questions.text:
A simple a.c. generator consists of a rectangular coil rotating in a magnetic field.
(a) State one change to the generator that would increase the induced potential difference.
(b) Explain why the output from the generator is alternating rather than direct.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Any one of: rotate the coil faster; use a stronger magnet; increase the number of turns on the coil. [1 mark]

(b) As the coil rotates, the rate at which it cuts through the magnetic field lines changes continuously [1 mark]. When the coil is perpendicular to the field it cuts lines at the maximum rate, inducing maximum p.d.; when it is parallel to the field it cuts no lines and the induced p.d. is zero [1 mark]. Because the direction of cutting reverses each half-turn, the direction of the induced current reverses, producing a.c. [1 mark].

Emerging: states the output reverses without explanation.
Mastering: links to the rate of change of flux explicitly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of practical electric motors has made a significant positive difference to people's lives. Give two specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: names one or two uses of electric motors without explaining the benefit.
Secure: names two applications (e.g. electric trains / trams reduce air pollution in cities; electric motors in medical equipment such as ventilators keep patients alive); explains the mechanism of the motor effect in each context (rotating coil in magnetic field).
Mastering: as Secure, plus evaluates whether the benefits outweigh any downsides (e.g. electricity must still be generated; rare earth materials needed for magnets); acknowledges that the impact was not immediately obvious when electromagnetic induction was first discovered.

[1 mark: named application 1 with benefit explained; 1 mark: named application 2 with benefit explained; 1 mark: motor mechanism linked to application; 1 mark: evaluation of impact/limitation; 1 mark: reference to how technology developed from scientific discovery]

practice_questions.text:
A transformer has 500 turns on its primary coil and 2500 turns on its secondary coil. The primary p.d. is 230 V and the primary current is 10 A.
(a) Calculate the secondary p.d.
(b) Calculate the secondary current, assuming the transformer is ideal.
(c) Explain why a step-up transformer is used at power stations before electricity is transmitted through the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\) → \(V_s = \frac{230 \times 2500}{500} = 1150\) V [2 marks: 1 for correct equation, 1 for answer]

(b) \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) → \(I_s = \frac{230 \times 10}{1150} = 2\) A [1 mark]

(c) Stepping up voltage to a high value reduces the current (\(P = IV\) — same power, higher V means lower I). Lower current reduces heat lost in cables (\(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\)), making long-distance transmission far more efficient. [2 marks: 1 for lower current argument; 1 for linking to \(I^2 R\) heat loss reduction]

Emerging: only states high voltage is used.
Mastering: chains the full argument — transformer equation → lower current → \(I^2 R\) loss reduction → more energy reaches consumers. [1 mark for clear logical chain]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between irradiation and contamination, and explain why contamination by an alpha-emitting isotope is considered more hazardous than irradiation by the same source.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear distinction — irradiation is external exposure that stops when the source is removed; contamination means radioactive material is in/on the body and continues to emit radiation (1). Alpha particles are highly ionising (1) but have very short range, so external alpha poses little risk to internal organs; if inhaled/ingested, alpha causes intense localised damage to surrounding tissue (1). Any relevant link to half-life of isotope determining duration of internal dose (1). Secure: Two valid points with some comparison. Developing: One correct distinction or one hazard point. Emerging: Vague or confused answer.

practice_questions.text: A hospital uses a PET scanner to detect the spread of cancer. Describe how a PET scan produces an image, including the type of radiation used and how the scanner detects it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Patient is given a tracer that emits positrons / beta-plus particles (1). Positrons annihilate with electrons in tissue, producing two gamma rays in opposite directions (1). External detectors on both sides record the paired gamma rays and build a 3-D image of tracer concentration (1). Secure: Two valid stages. Developing: One stage correct. Emerging: Simply names PET without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a long half-life makes a radioactive contaminant more dangerous than a short half-life contaminant, even if both initially have the same activity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Long half-life means the number of radioactive nuclei decreases slowly (1), so activity remains significant inside the body for a prolonged period (1), leading to a larger total radiation dose to surrounding tissue over time (1). Secure: Two linked points. Developing: States long half-life = stays longer, but does not link to dose. Emerging: Vague statement about danger.

practice_questions.text: A radiotherapy machine delivers a gamma-ray beam to a tumour from six different directions, all aimed at the same point. Explain why this multi-beam approach is used rather than a single beam.
practice_questions.marks: Each individual beam passes through different healthy tissue (1) so each region of healthy tissue receives a lower dose; the tumour receives the combined dose from all six beams and is more effectively destroyed (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during nuclear fission of uranium-235 and explain how this process can be made self-sustaining in a controlled nuclear reactor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A slow neutron is absorbed by uranium-235 nucleus (1); nucleus splits into two smaller daughter nuclei of roughly equal mass (1); releases kinetic energy of particles and gamma radiation (1); two or three neutrons are also released (1); in a reactor, control rods absorb excess neutrons so on average exactly one neutron per fission triggers the next event, maintaining a steady chain reaction (1); this controlled chain reaction releases energy at a constant rate for electricity generation (1). Secure: Four to five points with coherent explanation of chain reaction control. Developing: Describes fission but limited chain-reaction detail. Emerging: Names fission without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive tracer has a half-life of 110 minutes. A patient is given a dose at 9:00 am. Calculate how many half-lives have passed by 2:30 pm and state what fraction of the original activity is left at that time. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Time elapsed = 2:30 pm − 9:00 am = 5 hours 30 minutes = 330 minutes (1). Number of half-lives = 330 ÷ 110 = 3 (1). Fraction left = ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8 (1). So one eighth, or 0.125, of the original activity is left (1).

Common error: dividing the total time by the activity instead of counting the halvings.

practice_questions.text: A book has a mass of 0.8 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
Describe the difference between elastic and plastic deformation of a material when a stretching force is applied and then removed.
practice_questions.marks: In elastic deformation, the material returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed [1 mark]. In plastic deformation, the material is permanently changed and does not return to its original shape [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Defines elastic deformation correctly but does not address plastic deformation, or vice versa.

practice_questions.text: A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. A force of 5 N is applied to it. Calculate the extension of the spring. Then calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
practice_questions.marks: Extension: e = F ÷ k = 5 ÷ 40 = 0.125 m [1 mark]. Elastic PE: E_e = ½ × 40 × 0.125² = ½ × 40 × 0.015625 = 0.3125 J [1 mark — method mark for correct squaring]. Accept 0.31 J [1 mark for correct final answer with unit].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly calculates extension but makes an error in squaring the extension in the PE equation.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates a spring. She finds it obeys Hooke's law up to a force of 20 N. Beyond this, the spring becomes permanently deformed. The spring constant is 500 N/m. Calculate the maximum extension at which Hooke's law holds. Suggest what the force-extension graph would look like beyond this point.
practice_questions.marks: Maximum extension: e = F ÷ k = 20 ÷ 500 = 0.04 m [1 mark]. Below this extension the graph is a straight line through the origin (extension proportional to force) [1 mark]. Beyond 0.04 m, the graph curves upwards (less extension per unit force added, as the spring stiffens before breaking) or the material is permanently deformed [1 mark]. The extension cannot be recovered when the force is removed beyond this point [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct maximum extension, correct description of graph shape in both regions.
Developing: Correct extension but does not describe the graph beyond the limit.

practice_questions.text: A force of 250 N is used to push a heavy trolley 12 m along a corridor. Calculate the work done. If this is completed in 30 seconds, calculate the power.
practice_questions.marks: Work done = F × d = 250 × 12 = 3,000 J [1 mark]. Power = E ÷ t = 3,000 ÷ 30 = 100 W [1 mark]. State unit: 100 W (watts) [1 mark — mark can be within the calculation line].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly calculates work done but cannot calculate power or uses wrong time unit.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the following claim: 'A stiffer spring always stores more elastic potential energy for the same applied force.' Use the equation E_e = ½ke² to support or challenge the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Notes that for the same applied force F, a stiffer spring (larger k) produces a smaller extension (e = F/k). Substitutes into E_e = ½ke²: E_e = ½k(F/k)² = ½F²/k. This shows that for the same force, a stiffer spring actually stores LESS elastic PE (because k is in the denominator). The claim is therefore FALSE. For the same extension (not the same force), a stiffer spring stores more energy (E_e = ½ke², larger k → larger E_e). Clarifies the conditions under which each conclusion applies. Reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly identifies that the equation gives E_e = F²/(2k) for same force; concludes correctly that stiffer spring stores less energy for same force.
Developing: Uses E_e = ½ke² but does not substitute e = F/k to isolate the effect of k; gives a partially correct conclusion.
Emerging: States a conclusion without using the equation.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for average speed, including units for each quantity.
practice_questions.marks: Award: average speed (m/s) = distance (m) ÷ time (s). All three units must be present.

practice_questions.text: A cyclist travels 540 m in 60 s. Calculate their average speed in m/s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: correct substitution and answer 9 m/s with unit.
Secure: correct method, minor arithmetic error.
Developing: equation recalled but substitution error.
Emerging: equation not recalled.

practice_questions.text: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. Explain what acceleration means and calculate the car’s acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: explains acceleration as rate of change of speed (1), correct equation (1), correct answer 2.5 m/s² with unit (1).
Secure: correct calculation but incomplete explanation.
Developing: defines acceleration but calculation error.
Emerging: partial definition only.

practice_questions.text: A velocity–time graph shows a vehicle accelerating from 0 to 20 m/s over 10 s, then travelling at constant velocity for 20 s. Compare the gradient of the first section with that of the second, and calculate the total distance travelled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: gradient section 1 = 2 m/s² (1), gradient section 2 = 0 m/s² (1), area 1 = 100 m (1), area 2 = 400 m, total 500 m (1).
Secure: correct gradients, one area error.
Developing: gradient recognised but area method unclear.
Emerging: only one correct value.

practice_questions.text: A stone is dropped from a cliff and falls for 3 s before hitting the ground. Taking acceleration due to free fall as 10 m/s², calculate (a) the final speed of the stone and (b) the distance it falls. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) v = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s (1); (b) uses area = ½ × base × height or correct equation, distance = 45 m (1) with correct working (1) and units (1).
Secure: method correct, one calculation error.
Developing: one part fully correct.
Emerging: attempts equation but significant errors.

practice_questions.text: A student says that displacement and distance are the same thing. Explain why this statement is incorrect and give an example to support your explanation. Use your answer to compare the scalar and vector nature of these two quantities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: defines displacement as net distance with direction (vector) and distance as total path length (scalar) (2), correct distinguishing example e.g. running a lap of a track (2), clear explanation that displacement depends on start/end positions while distance depends on path (2).
Secure: correct definitions, example present but link to scalar/vector incomplete.
Developing: some correct ideas about direction, example vague.
Emerging: limited or confused definition.

practice_questions.text: State Newton’s first law of motion.
practice_questions.marks: Award: an object remains stationary or continues at constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant force. Accept equivalent correct wording.

practice_questions.text: A wave in a ripple tank has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.04 m. Calculate its speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: correct equation stated and correct answer 0.2 m/s with unit.
Secure: correct method, minor arithmetic error.
Developing: equation recalled but substitution error.
Emerging: equation not recalled or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². Explain what is meant by resultant force and calculate the resultant force acting on the car.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: resultant force defined as the net or combined force taking direction into account (1), F = ma stated (1), correct answer 3600 N (1).
Secure: correct calculation but incomplete definition.
Developing: definition given but calculation error.
Emerging: definition only or equation only.

practice_questions.text: A crumple zone at the front of a car extends the time for a collision from 0.05 s to 0.25 s. Compare the forces the driver experiences in each case if their change in momentum is 900 kg m/s. Explain your answer using physics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: F = Δp ÷ Δt used (1), force without crumple zone = 900 ÷ 0.05 = 18,000 N (1), force with crumple zone = 900 ÷ 0.25 = 3,600 N (1), clear explanation linking longer time to smaller force for same change in momentum (1).
Secure: both forces correct, explanation incomplete.
Developing: one force correct, method shown.
Emerging: equation stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A radio station broadcasts electromagnetic waves at a speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s with a wavelength of 1500 m. Calculate the frequency of the broadcast. Give your answer in standard form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: f = v ÷ λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 1500 = 2 × 10⁵ Hz, with unit.
Secure: correct method, arithmetic error.
Developing: equation stated but rearrangement incorrect.
Emerging: no valid method.

practice_questions.text: Newton’s second law can be expressed as \(F = ma\) or as \(F = \Delta p \div \Delta t\). Discuss how both forms are useful and explain how the concept of momentum helps engineers design safer vehicles. Use specific calculations or examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: both equations stated and linked (2), specific example of safety feature using \(F = \Delta p \div \Delta t\) with correct reasoning (2), quantitative or qualitative comparison of forces showing safety benefit (2).
Secure: both equations, good safety feature explanation, limited quantitative support.
Developing: one equation applied, partial safety reasoning.
Emerging: identifies that time affects force without using equations.
